en: The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Subāhu, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Great Master of the Transmission of the Teaching, the Subject Fǎtián, in obedience to the Imperial Decree.

Chapter One: Attaining Siddhi through the Assistance of a Victorious Master and Companion. At that time, the yakṣa lord, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, out of great compassion for future generations, emitted a thousand rays of light and remained with a focused mind.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Subāhu, regarding the meaning of success and non-success for all mantras and vidyās by those who maintain their recitation, paid single-minded homage to that lord of yakṣas, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, and addressed him with these questions:
"O Bodhisattva!..."
I observe that in this world there are practitioners who maintain the purity of the fast, cultivate with diligent application, and yet fail to achieve accomplishment in mantras and vidyās.
Just as the sun spreads its radiance so that there is nowhere it does not illuminate, I pray that you will take pity on us and explain the causes and conditions for this.
Why is it that although those practitioners of recitation are diligent, supreme, and foremost, they are unable to achieve success in the superior, middling, or inferior methods of the mantras?
Why is it that one practices the causes yet does not obtain the fruit? Is this due to karmic obstructions that have not yet been extinguished?
We pray that the Bodhisattva will explain the meaning of attaining accomplishment through such practice, as well as the meaning of non-accomplishment and all matters of obstructive difficulties.
“Bodhisattva! As the Buddha has said:
‘The illumination of wisdom can extinguish the darkness of delusion;’”
"If ignorance and darkness are not extinguished, clear wisdom may be abandoned.
How can one cause those who uphold and recite [the teachings] to be free from doubt regarding all practices?
"O Bodhisattva!"
Why is it that for those who perform practices such as recitation, retention, and homa, the various mantra-kings and holy sages do not grant them accomplishment?
We pray that the Bodhisattva, out of great compassion, will explain each point in detail so that there may be no further doubt.
“Bodhisattva! Is it that the power of this Dharma is incapable?
Or is it that what you have done was performed at an improper time?”
Is it because of one's spiritual lineage or lack thereof?
Is it due to omissions or redundancies in the words and phrases of the mantra?
Or is it because of negligence or disrespect in one's practice?
Is it because the offerings are incomplete?
We pray that the Bodhisattva will explain each of these various matters and their respective obstacles in detail, so that all practitioners may fully understand them.

At that time, having heard these words of right-minded benefit spoken by the Bodhisattva Subāhu, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, in an instant, closed his lotus-eyes of blazing light; after reflecting and observing, he addressed the Bodhisattva Subāhu, saying: "Subāhu!

Your great compassion benefits all sentient beings; this mind of yours is as pure as the full moon at night, its radiance brilliant and free from the veil of clouds, ensuring that all practitioners do not lose the right path and enter the realm of the Buddha to reach the other shore.

The deeds performed by a bodhisattva do not seek their own happiness; because they concern other sentient beings, they harbor no resentment or malice. They regard the suffering and affliction of others as their own suffering and affliction, and they find joy themselves when others find joy.
"Subāhu! I observe that your intention is for the sake of sentient beings; you ask about this meaning as if you were their own infant.
Listen attentively, and I shall explain it to you."

“Subāhu! What I have now spoken is based upon the words of the Buddha. If there are those who practice the supreme activity, cultivating the conduct of mantra and seeking accomplishment, they must distance themselves from all afflictions, give rise to deep faith, and resolve upon bodhicitta. They must revere the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, place their trust and respect in me, and further take refuge in the Great Vajra Family.”

Furthermore, one should distance oneself from the ten unwholesome courses of action; whatever arises through body, speech, and mind, one should always remain free from delusion, ignorance, and the conduct of false views. If one seeks karmic fruition, one must possess wisdom.

It is like a farmer who attends to his cultivation and sows parched seeds in fertile soil; although he exerts effort and the seasonal rains fall in abundance, because the seeds are parched, there is no way for them to sprout.

Ignorance and false views are likewise so; for any practitioner engaged in spiritual cultivation, one must first ensure that one’s own mind is free from such things as false views and ignorance, remaining unshakable and unwavering as one practices the ten wholesome dharmas, and even constantly practicing all wholesome dharmas.

Should there be celestial Māras, asuras, or any other classes of rākṣasas and various spirits who feed on flesh and blood, and who, with malicious and poisonous minds, roam the three realms to afflict and harm sentient beings, causing practitioners to become distracted—if there are practitioners who delight in my Dharma and cultivate the recitation and practice of the mantra rites, then upon seeing them, these beings will naturally be struck with terror and be unable to cause them harm.

If one wishes to cause various powerful celestial Māras, the planetary deities (grahas), and even various ghosts and spirits to be unable to create obstacles and to be subdued, one must enter that Samaya Great Maṇḍala.
Because one enters the dwelling place where those great powerful holy assemblies of devas reside, it is therefore called the Great Maṇḍala.

Furthermore, one must also enter the most excellent maṇḍalas of the Great Vidyārājas and Great Mantras; because one enters various such maṇḍalas, this constitutes entering the locus of the accumulation of merit belonging to those Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Great Vajra Families, and Great Vidyārājas.

This constitutes serving the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vidyārājas; by doing so, one immediately receives the protective shelter of the shadows of such Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, causing obstructive celestial Māras, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, ghosts, and the like to be unable to inflict harm or affliction. They will not dare to approach the place where the practitioner resides, but will naturally retreat and disperse, no longer creating obstacles or difficulties.

Regarding the methods for accomplishing the superior, middling, and inferior grades of practice, all worldly and supramundane mantras and so forth will be easily accomplished; this is because one repeatedly enters those various maṇḍalas and samayas, receiving the protection and empowerment of their holy power, whereby all malevolent intentions are naturally destroyed.

Once one has been able to enter that Samaya Great Maṇḍala, one must still give rise to a courageous mind and the bodhicitta, placing faith solely in the Buddha and having no faith in non-Buddhists, celestial māras, or the like.
If one recites my teachings while turning their back on this mind, they shall surely bring about their own ruin.

Furthermore, a practitioner who seeks to achieve accomplishment must first seek out a preceptor (ācārya) whose ethical virtue is pure and free from transgressions, and whose merit and fortune are most excellent.

If one receives these instructions from such an ācārya and maintains their recitation, and furthermore resolves one's own mind with courageous diligence in what is practiced, accomplishment will be easily attained and spiritual efficacy swiftly obtained.
For example, just as planting crops requires good soil, and when the earth is fertile, grain is easily obtained, so it is when one finds an excellent teacher.

"If, however, such a miraculous efficacy is difficult to find, this is due to past karma; one should instead seek out an excellent site and construct a stūpa by marking the sand or piling up earth. Within it, one should install an image and enshrine śarīra relics, making offerings with various kinds of incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, exquisite banners, pennants, canopies, and music. Furthermore, one should offer praise and perform repentance with focused and sincere devotion."
Once the repentance is completed, continue the recitation as before with focused concentration and without interruption; you will certainly obtain spiritual efficacy.
"In practicing in this manner, one must have companions; if there are no companions, the practice is deficient."
For example, for a chariot to travel, both wheels must be complete; if one is missing, there is no way to proceed. It is the same with the companions who assist in spiritual practice.

If you seek such companions, you should seek those of noble lineage, of handsome appearance, with unimpaired faculties, whose natures are gentle and pliant, who delight in cultivating wholesome dharmas, whose wisdom is clear and sharp, who are diligent and courageous, who possess great compassion, who always delight in giving, who have faith in and revere the Triple Gem, attending upon and making offerings to them, and who do not place their trust in other external paths, celestial māras, or the like.

One should know that these are companions for the cultivation of merit who dwell within this Bhadrakalpa; for all practitioners of recitation, they will swiftly attain accomplishment in their various practices.

2. Chapter Two: Selecting a Superior Location from the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Subāhu*. "Furthermore, if a practitioner who upholds the recitation wishes to cultivate the practice of mantra (*mantracaryā*) and seek accomplishment, they should first seek out the sites where the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas dwelt in the past as taught by the Buddhas; these constitute superior locations."
In such places as these, devas, nāgas, asuras, and others constantly provide protection, offerings, and reverence.
Why is this? Because they were formerly inhabited by the most holy beings among gods and humans.
Having obtained such a site, the practitioner who maintains the recitation must likewise purify body and mind and be fully endowed with moral discipline, dwelling constantly therein.

If such a blessed ground is unavailable, one may instead choose the bank of a great river, the shore of a small stream, or the side of a spring or pond; even a marsh or lake filled with clear water, provided it is free from venomous aquatic creatures, is acceptable.
Such a place should be strewn with lotuses, blue utpala flowers, various famous blossoms, exotic fruits, and soft grasses.
Alternatively, it may be in a mountain cave; such a place is pure and free from lions, wild beasts, or any other terrifying creatures.

Having found such a site, one must first excavate it to a depth of one cubit (*hasta*), removing thorns, shards, rubble, ash, charcoal, saline soil, husks, bones, hair, and any insect nests. Even if the excavation cannot be completed to that depth, one may discard that spot and seek another location. Once the excavation of one cubit has been made, fill it with clean earth and erect a dwelling upon it.

Using pure earth as mortar, they plastered and adorned both the interior and exterior; furthermore, they smeared the ground within with *kumuda* (coromandel) powder. They always sat and slept directly upon the ground, making no use of couches, beds, or similar furniture.
The doors of that chamber may only face east, west, or north; they must not face south.
Once the house has been thus constructed, one should install the honored image in that location according to the specific ritual activity to be performed.
Before placing the honored image, one should first adorn the location with various kinds of exquisite incense; the honored image may be carved, cast, or painted.

If it is to be painted, first seek out pure thread; select it so that all hair and impurities are removed, then weave it into a cloth of appropriate dimensions, ensuring the length and width are in proportion, and leave the threads at both ends intact without cutting them away.

Once the weaving was completed, it was soaked in scented water, stretched out again, and made perfectly straight. Then, the painters were required to eat vegetarian food and bathe; they further received the eight precepts so that they were pure both internally and externally, before they could direct their minds and take up their brushes.
All pigments used must be of the very highest quality; do not use animal-hide glue, but instead blend the pigments with various fragrant glues.
Once the painted image is completed and installed in its proper location, perform a grand offering with various kinds of food and drink, incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments.

If one lacks the power to perform an extensive rite, one should offer whatever is available; it is essential, however, to be single-mindedly devoted and sincere, placing faith, reverence, praise, prostration, and offerings before the image.
Having done so, whatever is sought before this image will be swiftly accomplished.
"When a practitioner of recitation is about to begin their practice, they must first shave their head and bathe, putting on new, clean garments.

These garments must not be made of silk, nor may they be white; one may use cloth, tree bark, or materials from plants and trees, which must then be dyed with red earth to alter their color. Furthermore, they must receive and maintain an alms-bowl."

The vessels may be made of sāla wood, earthenware, or even copper, iron, gourd, or calabash; they must be held upright, smooth, clean, and lustrous, and must not be porous, leaking, cracked, or broken.

Holding this alms-bowl, one should wander through the streets to beg for food. When begging for food, one should choose a village that is neither too near nor too far, where there are many śūdras, where the Triple Gem is revered, where food and drink are plentiful, and where there are no non-Buddhist practitioners or brahmins.
Because that brahmin was by nature shameless and shrouded in pride, he further acted as follows:

whenever he saw a practitioner of the Way carrying an alms-bowl, wandering for alms, cultivating the Buddha-dharma, and reciting mantras, he would give rise to anger and seek to obstruct him, saying to the practitioner:

"If you are of the original Brahmin caste, you should cultivate the Brahmin dharma; you must observe the six duties, pursue extensive learning and pure conduct, revere the various devas, serve the king as a minister, and you must also take a wife and father sons to continue the lineage."
"If practicing this constitutes your liberation, why do you recite the mantras of the Śākya teachings and faithfully practice the Buddha-dharma?
If the practitioner is of the Kṣatriya caste, he should say:
"You, being of the Kṣatriya caste, ought to uphold the royal law and succeed to the throne."
"How can one recite and uphold the mantras of the Buddhist teachings while turning one's back on one's own fundamental school in the pursuit of liberation?

He continued, "Even those of the Vaiśya and Śūdra castes all attain liberation by expounding the fundamental practices of their own schools; it is not fitting for them to recite Buddhist mantras to seek liberation. With the fire of anger burning their hearts, they employ various kinds of frivolous speech and many expedient means to create obstacles and hindrances, vexing and disturbing practitioners so as to cause them to retreat from their resolve."
"One who follows the path of correction begs for food at the proper time, unlike the non-Buddhists who eat after midday.
In all places where one begs for food, one must not go to the homes of non-Buddhists or to places where many non-Buddhists reside."
Regarding the principles of good and evil, cause and effect:
one who can cultivate wholesome dharmas shall realize nirvana;
if one commits evil karma, one will ultimately fall into the realms of suffering.
The fruits of good and evil do not depend on one’s lineage; they arise solely from the deluded discriminations of the world.
Furthermore, since beginningless time, sentient beings have possessed defiled bodies that cannot attain purity of body and mind through the purification of food alone.
Only by distancing oneself from all evils and constantly cultivating wholesome dharmas can one truly achieve purity of body and mind.
For example, it is like a person who, suffering from a physical ulcer, seeks medicine to apply to the wound solely with the hope of curing it, and not for any other purpose.
Likewise, when a practitioner eats food, they do so only to eliminate hunger, not for the sake of sensual gratification.

Furthermore, it is like a person who has fallen into a place of peril and, driven by hunger, kills and eats his own child; this is done to eliminate the suffering of hunger, not out of a craving for flavor. The practitioner’s eating of food is also like this.
The method of eating is like weighing an object: it is not the object that is light or heavy, but the scale itself that must be level and upright.
When a practitioner eats, it is likewise so: one must neither exceed the proper measure nor eat too little; one should simply take enough to sustain oneself, avoiding both hunger and over-saturation.
Furthermore, it is like replacing a pillar in a dilapidated house to avoid its collapse;
or like greasing the axle with oil, valuing the ability to move forward.
A practitioner’s eating is also like this: it is merely for sustenance, not for flavor. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Sentient beings of the desire realm subsist by means of nutriment.

Furthermore, although the practitioner consumes food and drink to sustain the body, they constantly contemplate this body as being like a plantain tree, devoid of solidity; thus they always restrain the mind and do not dwell in craving or attachment.

Whenever begging for alms, one should carry the bowl and proceed on rounds in proper sequence. One must constantly reflect upon what the World-Honored One has taught: to subdue the six sense faculties through wisdom and skillful means so that they do not become distracted. One should recognize that the exquisite forms and various sensory objects encountered are the realm of Māra, intended to delude the human mind.

When practitioners of the Way employ skillful means, it would be better for them to have their two eyes burned and pierced with red-hot iron than to look upon exquisite forms with a distracted mind—even toward extraordinary and diverse sensory objects—and rather to wander for alms according to circumstances without dwelling in attachment.

Constantly practicing such contemplation to subdue the mind, he silently begs for alms while wandering through the houses of others, remaining without superior, middling, or inferior states, and far removed from grasping or rejecting.

However, he does not go to the homes of those who have recently given birth, nor to places where many drink alcohol, nor to places where men and women are intoxicated and immersed in passion, nor to places where many children play, nor to gatherings of various groups of men and women, nor to places where male and female performers play music, nor even to places where there are vicious dogs; he should not go to any such locations.
"Having obtained food through alms, bring it back to your original place; wash your feet, spread out a seat, and only then may you eat.

Before eating that food, first divide it into three portions: one portion offer to the Honored One as an act of worship, one give to those without obstruction, and one consume yourself, eating at the proper time."
Upon finishing the meal, one must wash and rinse the mouth to ensure purity.

Furthermore, one must bathe three times a day; having first purified oneself, one should then offer various kinds of incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments, along with praise, prostrations, and offerings of all food and drink to the honored image. All such offerings must be scrupulously clean and free from any pungent or impure substances.
Whenever one performs recitation, one should sit upon *śarī* grass.
Regarding all offerings, even if one cannot provide them on a grand scale, one should simply present incense and flowers according to one's means.
These include *tagara*, *arkapuṣpa*, auspicious fruit (*bhadradāru*), *malhāta*, *śarī* grass, and lotuses; these should be combined for offering so that they are pleasing to the senses.
Whether walking or sitting, the practitioner should maintain the recitation and achieve mastery of the visualization; however, it is not permitted to recite while lying down.
Once the recitation is completed, one should constantly contemplate its merits during the six periods of the day, maintaining an uninterrupted mind and praying for its fulfillment.

3. Chapter on Distinguishing the Rosary and Maintaining the Mind Free from Obstacles, from the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Subāhu*, Part Three: "Furthermore, because afflictions such as desire conjoin with the mind, they are called saṃsāra. If the root afflictions are removed, it is like a pure crystal gem; if one is separated from saṃsāra, that is termed liberation."
Furthermore, just as water is inherently pure yet can be turbid by sediment in a single moment;
likewise, the source of the mind of sentient beings is inherently pure, yet in an instant it is defiled by various afflictions.

"Furthermore, it is said that there are many kinds of rosaries, namely those made of bodhi seeds, vajra seeds, lotus seeds, wood-apple seeds (*dhātrī*), as well as agate, various jewels, tin, lead, copper, and so forth. Having selected any one of these materials to serve as the beads and counting one hundred and eight, the practitioner who maintains the recitation should always cherish and protect them."

Whenever performing recitation, one should sit properly before the deity according to the ritual rules, subduing the sensory faculties. With the body upright and composed, one must not lean against anything. One should fix the mind upon the deity, the mantra, and the mudrā, withdrawing the consciousness so that it does not become distracted. Then, taking up the rosary, hold it in the right hand while supporting it from below with the left hand; for every single recitation of the mantra, move one bead. The total number of recitations must always be strictly determined, neither falling short nor exceeding the count.
Regarding the method of recitation: move the lips slightly so as not to produce sound, nor show the teeth; focus the mind single-pointedly without allowing it to wander.

The realm of sentient beings dwells in the station of ordinary persons; their minds are like monkeys, greedily attached to various objects, finding pleasure therein and refusing to let go, just as the great ocean, when stirred by the wind, gives rise to waves that cannot subside of their own accord.

Ordinary beings perceive objects in exactly this same way; they must always collect and withdraw their minds, not allowing them to become distracted or agitated, lest waves arise within the source of the mind.

If a practitioner reciting mantras becomes weary and feels the onset of drowsiness, fearing a loss of mindfulness, they should immediately rise to walk or gaze at the four directions to harmonize the spirit and thoughts, or wash their face and eyes with cold water. Once refreshed and alert, they may return to their seat and continue the recitation.
If the practitioner is afraid of toil and hardship and their mind wavers, they should form this thought: "This body has no master;
it is received as a result of karma. It is without support or fixedness, flowing and turning according to karma through the cycle of the eight sufferings. Where can one find escape?"
"As for cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and gadflies, fleas, mosquitoes, and horseflies—such afflictions are found everywhere.
Furthermore, if greed and desire are rampant, one should practice the contemplation of white bones and the impurity of decay;
if anger and hatred are rampant, one should practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion.
If ignorance is rampant, practice the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, if you encounter an enemy, contemplate them as a friend or spiritual mentor (*kalyāṇamitra*); or if a friend or spiritual mentor should suddenly become an enemy, contemplate them likewise.

When a practitioner encounters such objects as enemies or kin, they must not give rise to thoughts of discrimination, hatred, or attachment; rather, they should abide in equanimity and right mindfulness free from clinging.
Furthermore, when emerging from the maṇḍala, one must not speak with brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, and the like, nor should one speak with eunuchs, women, and so forth.
Why is this? Because they are not companions who delight in the Dharma;
one may speak with them using the same words as one's fellow practitioners and associates.
Or, when engaging in activities such as bathing, defecating, or urinating, one must enter the water to bathe and ensure cleanliness.

Or, one may offer incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments, along with hymns of praise and worship; furthermore, by observing the precepts, practicing with diligence, and reciting mantras, all wholesome dharmas are dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Just as all streams flow toward the ocean, and once they have entered the sea, they become one single flavor; so too do all accumulated roots of goodness converge toward the fruit of Buddhahood, with immeasurable masses of merit naturally following along.

It is like a person who plows a field and sows grain, intending only for the seeds and fruit, not for the stalks; once the seeds and fruit are abundant, the stalks exist naturally as a matter of course.
Seeking the fruit of Buddhahood is likewise so: all blessings and joys arrive of their own accord without being sought.
Furthermore, a practitioner of recitation should not, for the sake of the small, obstruct the great.
Or if someone comes to invite one, one should respond by saying:
"Wait until I have attained long life and all its requisites for happiness;
once this mind is fulfilled, I shall then be able to fulfill the wishes of all sentient beings."
"Furthermore, the practitioner must distance themselves from the eight worldly dharmas, namely: praise and blame, gain and loss, fame and infamy, and suffering and pleasure."
Such a Dharma cannot abide in the mind; it is just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse, nor do they coexist for even a single moment.
It is also like lighting a lamp within a room to ward off the wind: if the flickering is avoided, the light will become brilliant.

Just as a practitioner of mantra recitation must also apply diligent effort, so too will wholesome dharmas increase when their preparatory application is established. Furthermore, the practitioner of mantra recitation must maintain mental concentration;

they must not engage in singing, dancing, or frivolous entertainment; nor harbor pride regarding self or others, hold wrong views or perverse attachments, or succumb to envy, indolence, laziness, or sleep. They must likewise avoid entering festive gatherings, becoming intoxicated by perverse doctrines or meaningless discourse, and even such things as anger, harsh speech, and double-tongued talk—all such matters must be strictly avoided.

Furthermore, one must not consume food that has been offered as an offering or food left over by spirits or ghosts. The practitioner may eat only the "three whites," fruits from trees, roots of vegetables, milk, curd, and gruel; as well as barley flour cakes, oil-cake dregs, and various kinds of millet porridge.

Furthermore, the practitioner of recitation must diligently apply themselves day and night to recite according to the Dharma. They should always, with reverence, faith, and precious care, sincerely repent before the Buddhas, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the bodily relics, vowing that all prior transgressions shall be entirely extinguished.

Each time one performs the recitation, first invoke [the deity] according to the ritual; when the recitation is completed, perform the dedication of merit according to the ritual, and after making the aspiration prayers, finally dismiss [the deity].

Or when it is night and one is about to sleep, one should spread auspicious grass (*kuśa*) on the ground not too close and not too far from the side of the deity, and sit or lie upon that grass. Once seated, one should then give rise to a mind of benefit and happiness toward all sentient beings, perform the meditations of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, and thereafter sleep.
4. The Fourth Section on the Vajra-Piṇāka from the Sūtra Requested by Subāhu Bodhisattva: "I shall now explain in detail the dimensions of the various *vajras*."
Their length may be eight finger-breadths, ten finger-breadths, twelve finger-breadths, sixteen finger-breadths, or at most twenty finger-breadths; these five categories do not exceed this limit.
The materials for constructing a *vajra* may be either gold or wood, varying according to the specific purpose sought.
If one desires to achieve the true illumination of the Buddha-dharma, one should fashion the *vajra* from *bodhi* wood.
If one seeks to subdue the earth-dwelling deities and the vidyādharas, one should fashion a vajra from gold.
If one seeks great wealth and status, one should fashion a vajra from brass.
If one seeks to subdue dragons, it should be made of refined copper.
If one seeks to subdue asuras or enter the asura caves, it should be made of precious gems.
If one wishes to accomplish all dharmas, one may use gold, silver, and copper combined.

If one desires to accomplish long life, auspiciousness, freedom from illness, and abundant wealth and treasures, or even to subdue the various planetary deities (grahas), one may use khadira wood for the construction.
If one wishes to subjugate a yakṣī, one may fashion [the ritual object] from madhūka wood.
If one wishes to subjugate an enemy, one should use thorny wood.
If one wishes to subjugate an extremely wicked and harmful adversary, one may use human bone.
If one wishes to accomplish illusory arts (*māyā*), one should use crystal (*kāca*) to fashion [the image].
If one wishes to cause extreme mutual hatred and aversion, one should use *karañja* wood to fashion it.
If one wishes to raise an army for combat or to subjugate ghosts and spirits (*bhūta-graha*), one should use *vibhītaka* wood to fashion it.
If one wishes to achieve mastery over yakṣas, gandharvas, or asuras, one may use juniper wood or pine wood to fashion [the image].
If one wishes to achieve mastery over the affection and esteem of nāga maidens, one should use nāga wood.
If one wishes to achieve the power of transforming one's form, one may use clay or silver to fashion [the image].
If one seeks wealth, one should use *aśoka* wood to fashion it.
If one wishes to achieve victory over adversaries, one may use *maṅgalya* wood, *arjuna* wood, willow wood, or similar materials to fashion it.
If one wishes to seek the accomplishment of the aspirational intention (*āśaya*), one may use red sandalwood or white sandalwood to fashion it.

As previously described, all *vajras* must have five prongs and must not be deficient; if there is even slight damage, the rite will not succeed. Furthermore, they must be maintained through ritual service (*sevā*) so that they are radiant, pure, exquisite, majestic, and lovely.

"When reciting, first offer ointments and exquisite fragrant flowers as an offering; thereafter, generate a mind of vast compassion, hold a *vajra* in your hand, and according to the ritual, focus intently on reciting the mantra of your respective family until the prescribed number is completed, without omitting even a single repetition."

Having completed the full number of recitations at the appointed time, one should place that *vajra* beneath the feet of the Honored One, and further offer various exquisite flowers, scented unguents, and so forth, even prostrating oneself in worship.
If, when reciting, one does not hold a vajra in hand, the rite will ultimately not be accomplished.
If one recites again, one must perform it according to the previous sequence, without any omission or deficiency.

Furthermore, if there should be any deficiency regarding the various items for offering or the ritual procedures, one must perform the mudrā for each individual item to make the offering, and only then may one engage in recitation.

"In the rites of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there are many kinds of substances, namely: realgar, orpiment, ox-gall, yellow lead, and medicinal eye-salves; as well as medicines such as sweet flag (*achyranthes*), and various weapons and implements such as armor, spears, swords, lassos, and tridents."
These various methods of accomplishment possess three levels of efficacy.
Within the mantras and ritual procedures of the principal deities that have been taught, as well as within the methods for accomplishing all other mantras, none transcend these [three].

"Furthermore, when there are practitioners of vidyā-mantras in the world who recite mantras seeking accomplishment, there are then the Vināyakas who create obstacles; they watch for an opportunity according to the practitioner as he recites, enter his body, cause his mind to become like one intoxicated or deluded, and give rise to various illnesses—thus creating all manner of hindrances and difficulties."
Those who create obstacles consist of four classes:
first, the *cūḍāntaka*; second, the jackals (*śṛgāla*); [and so forth].
The third is called Single-Tusk;
the fourth is called Dragon-Elephant.
Each of these four classes has immeasurable pinnayakas as their retinue, who create obstacles and difficulties throughout various places upon the great earth.
"First, there is a leader of a faction named Aśoka; his followers number seventy million, and they create obstacles for those who recite the mantras spoken by the four World-Protecting Kings."
"Second, there is a leader of the *vighna* class named Gajamukha; his retinue consists of eighteen *koṭis*, and they create obstacles and difficulties for the mantras spoken by Maheśvara."

"Third, the lord of the Single-Tusk Family is named Lamba-keśa; his retinue consists of sixty koṭis. They create obstacles for those who recite the mantras spoken by such deities as Mahābrahmā, Śakra, Sūrya, Candra, Vāyu, and Nārāyaṇa."

"Fourth, the leader of the Naga-elephant family is named Mūrdhaṭaka; his retinue consists of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of padmas, and they create obstacles for those who recite the mantras taught in that Buddha's teaching."
Furthermore, there is a son of Hārītī named Priyaputra, who creates obstacles for those who recite the mantras taught by Pañcika.
Also, Maṇibhadra has a son named Pūrṇabhadra, who creates obstacles for those who maintain and recite the mantras taught within his own sect.

"These various Vināyakas each create obstacles within their respective families, desiring that the practitioner not attain accomplishment; at times they may even manifest as the principal deity of the mantra and come to the practitioner's location to receive offerings."
Then the original Lord of Mantras came to the ritual arena; having seen these events, he returned to his own palace and thought to himself:
"Why has the Tathāgata granted their wishes without repelling these [obstacles]?"
"Will they cause affliction and disturbance to practitioners who are engaged in correct cultivation, causing their recitations and merits to fail to achieve fruition?

Even Brahmā, Śakra, the various devas, and the nāgas cannot shatter the vow of that Piṇāka to create obstacles; only the Great Illuminating Mantra (mahāvidyā-mantra), possessing great power, can repel such obstructing Piṇākas.

All practitioners should recite according to the Dharma; once the required number has been completed, they should further accomplish the sublime maṇḍala and perform homa, so that the obstructing Vināyakas may be dispersed and driven far away.
