The Remainder of the Fourth Section on the Vajra-Piṇāka: "Furthermore, when the practitioner performs recitation, makes offerings, or even performs homa, if they do not act according to the ritual manual or omit the prescribed procedures, those who create obstacles will find an opportunity."
Furthermore, the mind of one who practices may lack determination and harbor doubts, thinking:
"Should this mantra be recited? Or thinking: [etc.]
"If one thinks, 'Can that mantra be recited?
then those who create obstacles will find their opportunity.

Furthermore, if the practitioner discusses mundane, trivial matters—such as farming or trade—which offer no benefit or purpose for one's own practice, those who create obstacles will find their opportunity."
That Piṇāka enters the body of the practitioner, following at every step to watch for his shortcomings, creating various obstacles and hindrances so that the Dharma practice does not succeed.
It is like a person walking along the bank of a river; while the body remains on the bank, its reflection falls into the water, following every inch of the stride without ever being abandoned.
The manner in which those obstructors enter the bodies of practitioners and do not abandon them is likewise.
There are some piśācas who, at the time of bathing, find an opportunity to enter the body;
there are some piśācas who, at the time of recitation, find an opportunity to enter the body.
Some may enter the body when one is asleep;
some may enter the body when incense and flowers are offered;
and some may enter the body during the performance of homa.

It is like sunlight shining upon a fire-crystal; through the convergence of causes and conditions, fire is produced. Likewise, when Piṇāyaka dwells within the body of a practitioner, he seizes upon their vulnerabilities to cause the mind to become distracted, thereby giving rise to the fires of greed, hatred, and ignorance.
"If Pinnayaka, while one is bathing, seizes an opportunity to enter the body of the practitioner, he will cause various afflictions to arise:
suddenly feeling hunger and thirst, craving food and drink, or giving rise to thoughts of indolence and laziness; or becoming addicted to sleep, or giving rise to anger and other such states."
"If a Vināyaka, seeking an opportunity during the offering of fragrant ointments, enters the body of the practitioner, he will cause various afflictions to arise:
either longing for one's native land or place of origin, or giving rise to thoughts of indolence, or giving rise to sensual desires and conceptualizations of exquisite objects."

"If Pinnayaka, while the incense is being burned, watches for an opportunity to exploit a lapse, he breaks through the earth and enters the body of the practitioner, thereby causing various afflictions to arise:
such as the birth of jealousy, the outbreak of anger, the emergence of wrong views, or thoughts of illicit lust, and so forth."

"If Pinnayaka seizes an opportunity during the offering of lamps and enters the body of the practitioner, he will cause the practitioner to develop a heart disease; the mind becomes stifled with pain until the heart is damaged."
"If a Pināyaka seizes an opportunity during the offering of flowers and enters the body of the practitioner, he will cause various afflictions to arise:
either a feverish heat in the body, or pain in the limbs and joints, or disputes with one's companions leading even to their separation."
"If a Vināyaka, while one is engaged in recitation, seizes an opportunity to enter the practitioner's body, he will cause various afflictions to arise for the practitioner:
either they will contract illnesses and suffer physical pain, or they will suffer from abdominal ailments and irregular diarrhea."

Furthermore, when all the Vināyakas enter his body, they cause the practitioner to give rise to various afflictions. As the māras become rampant, the mind becomes deluded, losing its sense of direction and perceiving various anomalous signs:
sometimes appearing to recite mantras, yet the speech is indistinct;
or wandering aimlessly without any apparent cause.
Some, with indecisive minds, give rise to false views;
some say there is no rebirth in heaven and no commission of sin;
others claim there is no practice and certainly no power of the sages.

Vainly reciting mantras, they undergo suffering and toil in vain; being neither virtuous nor evil, without cause or fruit—they utter chaotic speech and flowery words, all manner of things lacking constancy;
sometimes breaking off grass or trees with their hands, or playing with clods of earth; or grinding their teeth while asleep;

or falsely giving rise to lustful thoughts, conceiving love and pleasure for a woman who does not reciprocate the practitioner’s desire, or even if she does find pleasure in him, her own mind is not compliant, so that throughout the night he cannot sleep.
Furthermore, while falling asleep, one may immediately experience bad dreams, seeing oneself pursued by Śarabhas, lions, wolves, and dogs;
or seeing camels, donkeys, pigs, cats, jackals, and the like; or seeing vultures, egrets, foxes, and other such strange, flying birds.
Furthermore, he dreams of naked heretics adorning themselves with dry and wet bones;

or he dreams of people who are short and stunted with evil features, or people with white leprosy on their bodies, or people with red beards and ugly countenances; or he dreams of heaps of skulls and bones, dried wells, and dried ponds; or he dreams of ruined houses abandoned by people; or he dreams of wicked men holding spears, swords, and various weapons, intending to come and inflict harm.

"If one sees such things in a dream, one should know with certainty that those piśācas are creating obstacles. The practitioner reciting the mantra should then perform the rite of the wrathful deity Amṛtakuṇḍalī and recite his mantra to protect the body, so that all such piśāca-demons and obstructors are completely liberated and unable to cause harm or affliction."
If there are those who constantly maintain this mantra, no demonic obstacles shall find an opportunity to prevail.

Furthermore, if a practitioner who recites the mantra wishes to perform rites to dispel demonic obstacles and seek liberation, they should first invite a pure and majestic ācārya to a mountain, the side of a pond, beneath a forest tree, an empty dwelling in a village, or a pure crossroads.
Having secured this location, one should then construct a maṇḍala using five-colored powders.
The five colors are yellow, blue, red, white, and black.

The dimensions of that maṇḍala shall be four cubits square, with four gates; in its center, one should construct a pit two cubits square, upon which to spread auspicious grass (kuśa). Outside the pit, on all four sides, one should arrange and install the seats for the vidyārājas who are the lords of mantras.

Furthermore, one should fashion the deities of the respective directions as powder-images in the eight directions. Use four precious vases, or alternatively, substitute them with four new earthenware vases; however, these earthenware vases must not be black, nor excessively burnt, nor underfired.

Fill a vase with the five grains, the five treasures, and scented water until it is full; additionally, insert red lotuses and branches from various trees into the vase, and further wrap the neck of the vase with thread of five colors. Place it in one of the four directions for use in the consecration ceremony.
Once they have been installed, one may then invoke the various vidyārājas and others, making offerings to them with exquisite incense, flowers, food, drink, and ritual implements.

Furthermore, one should offer wine, meat, radishes, fruits, vegetables, and the like to the deities of the eight directions and to the various Vighnas and Pināyakas who create obstacles. Thereafter, the person afflicted by the obstacle sits facing east within a pit in the center of the mandala. The Ācārya takes a flask from each of the four directions and recites the mantra of the wrathful deity Amṛtakuṇḍalī one hundred times to empower that flask. Once the recitation is complete, he performs the various ritual acts according to the dharma. Then, he pours the water from this flask upon the crown of the head of the person afflicted by the obstacle, and that person immediately attains liberation.

"This maṇḍala not only liberates one from demonic obstacles, but can also extinguish all sins and increase immeasurable merit; if one practices according to the ritual instructions, there is no result that cannot be attained."

Chapter Five: Distinguishing the Signs of Siddhi, from the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Subāhu*. "At that time, if a practitioner of mantra recitation is afflicted by various demonic obstacles and disturbances intended to cause them to retreat from their resolve, they must recognize these as demons and immediately perform the ritual methods to eliminate and resolve them. Once they have been eliminated and resolved, their body and mind will become tranquil, free from affliction and defilement."

Just as when the bright moon is freed from the dispersal of clouds, it leaves behind all obstructions and stands luminous in the expanse of the sky, shining unimpeded; so too is it for the practitioner who, through recitation and cultivation, attains liberation from demonic obstacles.

Furthermore, regarding those who recite mantras but fail to attain accomplishment: it is like a seed that, depending on the earth and the season, and provided that the wind and rain do not fail and the irrigation is not lost, may sprout and eventually reach maturity.
If a seed is not sown in the ground at the proper time, there is no way for its sprouts and stems to grow, let alone its branches, leaves, and fruits!

"If a practitioner of recitation does not follow the ritual rules and is not pure, if they have never been reverent or clean regarding the various offerings, if there are omissions or additions in the syllables of the mantra they recite, or if even their inhalation and exhalation are erroneous, abbreviated, or incorrect—for these reasons, the various siddhis do not manifest before them, and likewise, they fail to attain accomplishment."
Furthermore, just as when clouds arise and rain falls, its abundance or scarcity corresponds to the merit of sentient beings;
so too, the attainment of accomplishment follows the diligence and effort exerted by the practitioner who recites the mantra.

If a practitioner obtains such a superior site and adheres to the ritual procedures, remaining free from transgressions regarding what has been prescribed, their dark karma will be extinguished and their white karma will gradually increase; thus, whatever they seek through recitation will swiftly attain accomplishment.
If one acts in this manner such that there is no deficiency in each and every detail, one will attain all accomplishments without doubt.

Furthermore, if during the recitation there are omissions or transgressions—such as interrupting the primary recitation to hold other mantras, or bestowing the recited mantra upon those who are not like-minded—the recitation, though completed in number, will yield no result. In such a case, one should again cultivate a devout mind with double the previous intensity of focus, making offerings according to the ritual three times daily, purifying both the internal and external, and without failing in the prescribed etiquette, recite the mantra one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) times more.
Once the required number has been reached, one may perform the homa rite as an offering.

One should use either barley, or rice blossoms, or sesame seeds, or white mustard seeds, or lotuses—whichever of these is employed—and mix it with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Recite [the mantra] four thousand times, or seven thousand, or eight thousand, or even ten thousand times. Furthermore, take any one of the following types of wood for fuel: *utpala* wood, *bodhi* tree wood, white or red *ariṣṭa* wood, *nāga* tree wood, *aśoka* tree wood, *śrīvṛkṣa* wood, *eryarudha* wood, *campaka* wood, *khadira* wood, *śamī* wood, *plakṣa* wood, *apāmārga* wood, *mudu* wood, or *jambu* wood. Take whichever of these woods is available to serve as the sacrificial fuel.
Those that are moist may be used, but those that are withered, worm-eaten, hollow, or charred must not be used.

The firewood should be as thick as a finger and twelve fingers long; having cut it, one should smear both ends with ghee, honey, and curd, and burn it together with any one of the following—rice-pollen, sesame, or mustard seeds—to perform the homa.

Once the aforementioned number has been completed, one’s previous omissions and transgressions will be purified; only then may one further seek the siddhi of mantras, attaining it without obstacles or difficulties.

"Furthermore, if the mantra or vidyā held by the practitioner is restrained or bound by another division, or if it is severed or destroyed such that its desired goal cannot be accomplished, one should fashion an image of the deity and place it beneath the feet of the principal deity of that division. Facing each other, one should recite the wrathful mantras of great majesty belonging to the various divisions. Furthermore, one should bathe the deity with ghee, honey, and curd three times daily for ten days; thus, those restraints and bindings will naturally be liberated."

"Furthermore, if a practitioner has personally examined their recitation of mantras and the performance of their practice and finds no deficiencies, yet the sought-after *siddhi* is still not achieved, it must be that there is some lapse in the ritual. However, even if one does not know for certain what the specific obstacle is, provided one increases their diligence and remains untiring day and night, the tutelary deity will naturally appear in a dream to explain the cause of the hindrance; such a response is as predictable as the limits of the ocean tides."

In truth, the lords of mantras and vidyās of the various sections are certainly not mutually destructive and can never be suppressed or bound by one another. It is like two people who have become close friends and agree upon this one condition:
"From this day forward, do not go to such-and-such a house, nor engage in conversation with that person."
Yet, because of their mutual respect, that friend ultimately never went to him nor spoke with him.

The method of mantra recitation is likewise so: for this reason, a practitioner must not destroy one another’s mantras or vidyās, nor should they mutually bind or restrain each other, even to the point of performing non-virtuous acts such as homa.

"Furthermore, the practitioner should not transmit the mantra-maṇḍala with additions or omissions, nor should they exchange this rite for that one. One should not, without cause, strike or bind sentient beings; one should not perform homa to damage their limbs or even kill them to harm sentient beings. One should not destroy ghost clans or punish dragon species. One should not arbitrarily perform acts such as binding all ghosts, spirits, and constellations. Nor should one use dhāraṇī-rites to treat the illnesses of infants, thereby obstructing great matters."

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of attaining accomplishment as taught by the Vidyādharas and the various Vidyādhara schools, the required dharmas differ. Some state that one must possess ten dharmas to attain *siddhi*: namely, the practitioner, the assistant, the object to be accomplished, diligence, the location, the superior site, the season, the deity, the mantra, and material resources. When these ten dharmas are complete, *siddhi* is achieved.
Furthermore, other schools maintain that siddhi is accomplished by means of three factors: namely, the mantra, the practitioner, and the assistant.
Yet another school maintains that it is accomplished by means of four factors: namely, diligence, an auspicious day, an auspicious time, and the appropriate location.
Furthermore, one school asserts that five factors must be present for success, namely: the deity, the mantra, the location, the requisite wealth, and the object to be accomplished.

Another school asserts that ten factors must be possessed; another asserts that eight factors must be possessed; and others assert five, four, three, or even two factors, each establishing a fixed standard within their own tradition.
"In the fundamental school of our Buddha's teaching, we of the Vajra family must possess two factors for siddhi to be accomplished: first, the practitioner; second, the mantra."

First, as for the practitioner: they are fully endowed with the virtue of the precepts and practice right diligence and vigor; they do not give rise to greed or envy regarding the fame or profit belonging to others, and they have no stinginess toward their own wealth or even their own life.

2. Regarding the mantrin: when reciting the mantra of one's own chosen family, one should ensure that the syllables are complete and the vocal characteristics are distinct; all methods for seeking accomplishment must be fully possessed without any deficiency.

Furthermore, one must first obtain a place where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have previously resided; having obtained such a place, by reciting the mantra according to the Dharma, one will certainly attain the fulfillment of one's aspirations.
By accomplishing these two dharmas, one will certainly attain siddhi.

Furthermore, regarding the method for the practitioner’s recitation: it is like a lion, when driven by hunger, seizing and eating an elephant; it must first exert itself with full force and power. Whether seizing a sheep, a deer, or other small animals, the force and power displayed are identical to those used for an elephant.

When a practitioner recites mantras to seek the superior, middling, or inferior accomplishments, they must be diligent and courageous like a lion king; likewise, they must remain free from dualistic conceptualization.

"When a practitioner of recitation is engaged in their practice while staying in a city, a walled town, or a marketplace, they may encounter fleas, lice, mosquitoes, and gadflies that bite and suck their body; furthermore, they may see women adorned with clothing, bracelets, and earrings, or hear the various sounds of their jeweled necklaces."

If one dwells in deep mountains or vast forests, there will be fluctuations of cold and heat, or the onset of illness that afflicts both body and mind; furthermore, there may be fierce and evil beasts that come to harm people, causing them to give rise to fear and terror.
If one dwells by the seashore, one will see the wind driving the seawater to form great waves and billows; their harsh sounds terrify people, causing them to give rise to fear and dread.
If one dwells beside rivers, streams, ponds, or lakes, there will be snakes, insects, and venomous stingers—creatures that harm human beings.

If a practitioner of recitation intends to perform their practice in such a place, they must first understand that all such occurrences are demonic obstacles. Should they encounter these events, they must exercise patience so as not to allow the mind to become distracted by external conditions; alternatively, they may seek out a superior location to advance their spiritual cultivation. One must not give way to despondency upon meeting such circumstances, but rather must resolve to generate even more firm and courageous intent.
If one should have a regressive mind, there is fear that deviant thoughts will arise;
if deviant thoughts arise, one will surely be taken advantage of by evil Māras.

A wise person employs skillful means to bestow happiness upon sentient beings, ensuring that no class of sentient beings incurs transgression on this account and must suffer the bitter fruits of their actions.

"Furthermore, the practitioner must not recite too hurriedly, nor should they be too slow; the voice should be harmonious and flowing, neither too loud nor silent. Moreover, one must not allow the mind to dwell on other objects or engage in idle conversation with others, which would cause interruptions in the recitation."

Furthermore, one must not allow any omissions or errors in the words and phrases of the mantra; for if the words and phrases are deficient, the underlying principles will be distorted, making it difficult to achieve siddhi, precisely because of this.
It is like a traveler walking against the current; by avoiding such faults, one will swiftly obtain spiritual efficacy.

Furthermore, it is like the flow of a river that never ceases day or night; the practitioner who recites likewise remains uninterrupted throughout the day and night, and their merit increases just as that river rushes toward the great ocean.
Furthermore, if the practitioner’s mind comes into contact with defiled objects and gives rise to attachment, they will consequently fall into indolence;

recognizing this as the work of Māra, they must swiftly turn their minds back. They should close both eyes and perform visualization, either focusing on the syllables of the mantra or contemplating the deity, binding the mind so that it does not become distracted.
If, upon subsequently encountering such objects, the mind remains unmoved, this practitioner attains the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, for a practitioner reciting mantras who seeks *siddhi*, the essential requirement is to collect the mind and fix it upon a single object. If the mind is tamed, the body naturally abides in stillness; when the body is free from agitation, the mind becomes increasingly joyful. When body and mind become as one, this is called attaining *samādhi*.
When a practitioner of recitation attains this meditative mindfulness, all sins of the past and present are completely extinguished.
Once the sins have been extinguished, body and mind become transformed and purified; there will be no doubt that whatever undertakings one performs will achieve success.
The Buddhas have said:
"Of all phenomena, the mind is the root.
If the mind is not pure, one will experience the fruits of poverty and ugliness, or fall into the realms of hell or animals.

If the mind is pure, one shall attain rebirth in the heavens and among humans to experience happiness; eventually, one shall transcend the pleasures of earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as birth, old age, sickness, death, impermanence, non-self, and decay, and thereafter attain the bliss of liberation, quiescence, and *nirvāṇa*.

"Furthermore, all phenomena arise from the mind; they do not exist spontaneously, nor are they produced by time, nor born of Īśvara, nor are they without causes and conditions. Rather, conditioned by ignorance, one wanders through birth and death. Through the combination of the four great elements, there is that which is conventionally designated as 'form. Form does not possess a self, and the self does not possess form; form has no 'mine,' and the self has no possession of form. Thus, these four aggregates are ultimately and entirely empty."
Form is like a mass of foam; feeling is like a floating bubble; perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like a mirage or a magical illusion.
If one can attain such a vision regarding these phenomena, it is called right view;
if one gives rise to a contrary view, it is called wrong view.
"Furthermore, when the practitioner of mantra-recitation has completed the required number of recitations, how can one know that their practice is close to *siddhi*?
If, during sleep, they invariably experience auspicious dreams."
If one dreams that they obtain banners, streamers, and precious parasols, and are led into a most sublime palace; or ascend a multi-storied pavilion, climb a high mountain, or mount a great tree;
or further dream of riding upon a lion, a white elephant, a white horse, a white ox, or a rhinoceros, a yellow cow, a śarabha, and so forth;
or further dream of hearing the sound of great thunder in the sky;

Furthermore, one may dream of receiving the joyful favor of others who bestow fragrant flower garlands and fresh, clean garments; or obtaining water-born fruits or five-colored lotuses; or obtaining an image of the Buddha or the Buddha’s *śarīra*; or obtaining Mahāyāna sūtras; or seeing oneself in a great assembly sitting and eating together with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Or one may see oneself entering a stupa-temple or a monastic cell;

or see the Tathāgata seated upon a jeweled throne preaching the Dharma to the eight classes of gods and dragons (*deva-nāga-aṣṭakula*), while one enters the assembly and likewise sits to listen to the Dharma.

Or one may see a Pratyekabuddha preaching the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination; or see a Śrāvaka monk preaching the Dharma of realizing the four fruits; or see a Bodhisattva preaching the Dharma of the six *pāramitās*; or see various devas describing the joys of the heavens.
Sometimes they see upāsakas preaching on the method of wearying detachment from the household life; or they see upāsikās preaching on the method of wearying detachment from womanhood;

or they see kings, or pure-practicing brahmins, or extraordinary men, or beautiful women, or wealthy elders, or ascetic sages, or vidyādhara sages, or those who skillfully maintain the recitation of mantras;

or they see themselves swallowing the sun and moon; or they see their bodies crossing the great ocean, as well as rivers, streams, springs, and ponds; or they immediately drink all the aforementioned waters until none remain.
Some see fire issuing from their heads, or see themselves entering a great mass of flames;
furthermore, they dream of a large carriage filled with goods, drawn by both oxen and calves;
or they dream of obtaining a white fly-whisk, or leather sandals, or a sword, or a fine fan, or gold, jewels, cat's-eye gems, pearls, and necklaces.
Furthermore, if one sees one's own parents, or sees beautiful young maidens adorned with various jewels, or even obtains exquisite food and drink—
if one obtains such auspicious and favorable dreams as these mentioned above— one should exert oneself with diligence, and be joyful and courageous.
Why is this? One should know that within one month, half a month, a single day, or even a single kṣaṇa, one will certainly attain the vast siddhi.

Chapter Six: The Section on Knowing Proximity to Siddhi from the *Sūtra of the Questions of Subāhu Bodhisattva*. "Furthermore, the practitioner examines himself and finds that his power of recitation is effective; he feels redoubled joy and affection. His mind does not cling to objects of defilement, and he does not give rise to thoughts regarding various transgressions. He is naturally free from the afflictions of cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, and even such things as mosquitoes, gadflies, flying insects, and even venomous blood-eating snakes cannot harm him."

Furthermore, hungry ghosts (preta), piśācas, kaṭapūtanas, and the like, all dared not approach or harm the shadow of the practitioner; they faithfully accepted and followed every word and instruction spoken by the practitioner.

Furthermore, his intelligence and wisdom became doubly keen; he was well-versed in the meanings of texts, scripts, and commentaries, took delight solely in all wholesome dharmas, and exerted himself with diligent vigor.
Furthermore, they shall behold the treasures hidden within the earth as if there were no obstructions.

Their bodies will be free from illness and untainted by dust or grime; their bodies will emit fragrant scents, and all will find delight in them. Those who see or hear of them will all be filled with joy.
Furthermore, women devoid of lustful desires come to flatter and seduce him.
Because his body and mind are pure, he hears the voices of the devas in the air, or sees the bodies of those devas, and even sees the classes of asuras, gandharvas, and yakṣas.

If the practitioner of recitation encounters such auspicious signs, they should rejoice, knowing for themselves that they are close to attaining the siddhi of the mantra; they must then prepare the necessary ritual implements for the rite of accomplishment.

"Furthermore, when a practitioner wishes to initiate the attainment of *siddhi*, they must first fully observe the eight precepts for four days, or three days, or for two full days and nights; furthermore, they must abstain from food before seeking *siddhi*."
At that time, having heard these words from the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Subāhu remained silent for a moment and then addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying: “O Bodhisattva!
Previously, it was stated that purity is not attained through fasting; why then do you now advocate for the practice of fasting?
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"A person's eating of food is like lubricating a cart; if the cart is not lubricated, it is difficult to move forward."
"What is the meaning of this? At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva spoke these words in a voice like thunder: "I do not speak thus for the sake of purifying the mind;

rather, it is because the physical basis of sentient beings is inherently impure. It is composed of semen and blood, forming bones, marrow, flesh, and skin; there are head hair and body hair, eyes, face, ears, and nose; there is fat, the stomach and spleen, saliva, mucus, spittle, and even excrement and urine. These nine orifices flow together, and such various impurities of the bodily constituents all circulate and transform according to earth, water, fire, and wind."

If one seeks siddhi, one must first be pure; for at the time of accomplishment, one does not wish for urine or feces to flow out. Therefore, it is said that one seeks purity by abstaining from food; such matters are not taught as obstacles to the Path.
Thus purified, the body attains peace and bliss; at the time of accomplishment, one is spared from defilement.
Furthermore, if at this time the practitioner should suddenly give rise to afflictions and desire, they must immediately employ wisdom to perform visualization, thinking:
"This body is composed of impurities and is sustained merely by the consumption of flavors."
When one forms such a thought, the previously arisen conceptions are extinguished at that very moment; even regarding body, life, and wealth, there is no longer any stinginess or attachment.
It is just as when the sun rises, all the immeasurable darkness of the night is completely dispelled—it is exactly like this.
If the practitioner reaches this stage of cultivation, they should know for themselves that *siddhi* is not far off.

Furthermore, having gained such knowledge, on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the waxing moon, one should take pure earth and mix it with fresh, pure *gomaya*, applying it to the ground. Next, cleanse the ground by smearing it with incense; once the seats for the noble ones have been purified, arrange them so that all those noble beings face east, and then successively present offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, food, and drink.

First offer to the Buddha; next, offer to the Lord of the Family Mantra of the Great Vajra Clan; then, offer to the Lord of the Mantra one maintains. Having thus successively made offerings and praises to each—from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas down to the Lords of Mantras—once again arouse the great bodhicitta and the mind of great compassion for the sake of delivering all sentient beings from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

Having formed this thought, he further recited the Mahāsamāja Sūtra, the Śrī-gāthā Tathāgata-rahasya-mahājñāna-dīpa Sūtra, and the Parama-dharmacakra-pravartana Sūtra; having thus recited these sūtras either in their entirety or following one after another, he then bound the boundaries of the eight directions, the earth realm, and the space realm.

Just as the outer walls of a human dwelling protect against evil, so too does the establishment of the boundary (*sīmābandha*) ward off Māras; it shall ensure that those with malicious intent, including the obstructing celestial Māras, Asuras, and all spirits and ghosts, are unable to approach.
Furthermore, one should recollect the Armor Mantra to protect oneself.

I have already explained various maṇḍala rites; one should construct a maṇḍala using powders of five colors according to the requirements. Once it is made, first perform the rite for the guardians of the eight directions as desired, for those deities are able to destroy all who create obstacles and difficulties.

Furthermore, one should draw vajras, tridents, and so forth at the four corners of the maṇḍala. Then, reciting the mantra for offering the lion throne, place a seat of *kuśa* grass in the center of the maṇḍala. Take the substance to be accomplished, first place it within three *bodhi* leaves, and subsequently cover it with four *bodhi* leaves before setting it upon the seat. Then, consecrate it by sprinkling scented water empowered by mantras to eliminate demonic obstacles.

Then, sitting on the left side, one should recite the appropriate mantra. After a short while, one must again purify with scented water. Thereafter, one should perform one thousand *homa* offerings according to the appropriate ritual, reciting with single-minded devotion without interruption until the three signs appear; this constitutes the attainment of the accomplishment of the rite.
"The three signs are the sign of heat, the sign of smoke, and the sign of flame.
If one attains the sign of heat, one shall obtain all that is cherished and esteemed in the world;
if one attains the sign of smoke, one shall obtain the power of invisibility."
If one attains the sign of the flame, one shall attain a transformed, subtle body and become a vidyādhara, flying through the void with a long lifespan. As for attaining the sign of siddhi:

it is like a person reaching death, where the sensation of cold enters the body and pervades the entire frame; or like the intermediate state (antarābhava) entering the womb, which the pregnant woman perceives within herself.
Furthermore, it is like various fragrances in the world: when a person suddenly smells them, although the fragrance can be perceived, it has neither form nor shadow.
It is also like a fire-gem (maṇi) that, when illuminated by sunlight, causes fire to flow forth because the sunlight has entered it.
The entry of the *siddhi* into the body of all practitioners is likewise so.

Those external objects and images previously accomplished, or those internal mental representations sought by the practitioner for accomplishment, serve as specific manifestations; if that reciter focuses with uninterrupted concentration, they will certainly experience spiritual efficacy.

"One who attains *siddhi* may see the image being worshipped vibrate; or the hair-tuft on its face emit radiant light; or the body of the image tremble; or flowers descend from the sky; or at times, when there are no clouds, a fine rain falls; or a sublime fragrance descends; or the earth shakes; or one hears the spontaneous sound of celestial drums; or sees devas, asuras, and others dwelling in the void; or hears the voices of various devas and humans speaking; or hears the sounds of various great ornaments, necklaces, bracelets, and armlets; or sees the flames of the lamps increase in brilliance and become pure golden in color; or even when the oil is exhausted, the flames burn even more fiercely; or hears a voice in the air commanding one to state the vow sought; or feels all the hairs on the body stand on end."

Once such signs have appeared, one may be certain that the sought-after *siddhi* will be accomplished. At that time, one should fill a superior, pure vessel with fresh flowers, grind various fragrant waters, and add the five precious gems; combining these, one should prepare *arghya* water. Kneeling on one knee, one should offer it to the *iṣṭadevatā*, recite the mantra, and even extend praise through sublime verses. One should then give rise to a heart of joy and right faith, practicing with diligence and without slackening, performing prostrations and making offerings.
Having performed this, one shall state each of the matters sought; the Noble One’s mind being uninterrupted, whatever is requested will surely be granted.

Once the wish has been fulfilled, one should focus the mind single-pointedly, expressing faith, joy, and praise toward the *iṣṭadevatā* (Principal Deity). Then, once again offer *argha* water as an offering, recite the mantra of the Principal Deity, and further recite the dismissal mantras of the various families. Having recited the mantras according to the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), one should prostrate and request the worthy sages (*ārya*) to each return to their original positions.

7. The Seventh Chapter: The Section on Explaining Accomplishment. As asked by the Bodhisattva Subāhu. "Furthermore, although the practitioner may achieve the desired accomplishments through focused recitation and diligent, tireless application, they must at all times constantly maintain their mental attention."
Why is this? Because all those extremely wicked spirits and ghosts, due to their evil karma, do not wish for the practitioner to achieve success;

yet, if they were to achieve it, then within a range of either one hundred or one thousand *yojanas*—by the power, majesty, and presence of that mantra—no demons, ghosts, or spirits would dare to approach or invade.
They will think: "This practitioner has brought me no benefit in this life or in future lives.
For this reason, the practitioner must always remain mindful.

It is like a person who, clad in armor and mounted upon an elephant, further takes up bows, arrows, and various weapons to enter a great battle array; when those enemies see such majesty and ferocity, they retreat and flee far away, with none daring to face him.

If a practitioner of recitation constantly maintains their recitation without deficiency in the Dharma, and does not commit even the slightest transgression against the precepts—wherein the precepts are likened to armor, the mantra to a bow and arrow, and valor to riding an elephant—if one is thus endowed, it is likewise the case that evil spirits, demons, and gods will not dare to approach or invade them.

"Furthermore, when a practitioner seeks the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of Vetāla, they must seek one that is undecayed within a śmaśāna. That corpse must still have its limbs complete and possess the full characteristics of a man; moreover, one must not use one who is hunchbacked, crippled, lame, or deformed, nor one who is excessively fat or excessively thin, or any that are incomplete. Even corpses of those lacking the superior or middling grades of appearance are all unfit for use."
If one selects a person who possesses the marks of the highest grade, that is most excellent.

Furthermore, those who suffer from wind-disorders (*vāta*), malaria, dysentery, or malignant sores, or even those who have died after being bitten by snakes or insects in water or on land, with the poison spreading throughout their bodies and causing them to foam at the mouth—such individuals as these are all unfit for use.

Once a corpse has been selected, one must have companions hold clubs to guard it from day until the end of the night. Whether staying in the charnel ground itself, seeking out a secluded hut elsewhere, beneath a solitary tree, at a crossroads, beside a spring or pond, or within a mountain of jewels—if such a superior and excellent location is obtained, that Vetāla will certainly be able to be swiftly accomplished.

"In accordance with the aforementioned superior sites, one should select a pleasing location; once that site has been purified according to the ritual, one should further smear the ground with a mixture of pure earth and cow dung. When the ground is thus purified, one should construct a samaya-maṇḍala using five exquisite powders—blue, red, white, black, and yellow."
I have already previously explained the various names of these maṇḍalas.

Within any of these maṇḍalas, one may construct whichever maṇḍala is appropriate; within that maṇḍala, one should arrange four auspicious vases (kalaśa). Fill each vase with water until it is full, or alternatively, use bitter water. Then, insert seasonal vines or various extraordinary flowers into the vases.

Having performed these rites within the maṇḍala in this manner, one should cause the assistant to arouse a spirit of heroic resolve and not feel any fear. First, one should purify the hair of the corpse; then, bathe it with water from an auspicious vase (bhadraghaṭa) to make it clean. Afterward, anoint it with oil, and once the anointing is complete, wrap it in a high-quality white cloth.

When this has been completed, one should spread auspicious grass (*kuśa*) within the maṇḍala that has been prepared and scatter various flowers; then, have the assistants carry this corpse together and place it within the maṇḍala.

Either facing east or facing north, one should install [the image] according to the ritual rules. Thereafter, one should make offerings with unguents, incense, flowers, garlands, and even wine, meat, and various kinds of food; if one cannot provide these extensively, it is sufficient to do so according to one's own capacity.
Nevertheless, one should perform the recitation using the mantra of the specific family and root deity corresponding to this maṇḍala.

Furthermore, regarding this mantra-vidyā-lord of one's own family, one should give rise to faith and venerate it with sincere devotion; relying upon the ritual procedures, one should focus single-mindedly on its recitation to seek accomplishment.

Furthermore, there are various *bhūtas* that move invisibly to create obstacles, as well as *nāgas*, *bhairavas*, and others; the practitioner should first scatter offering substances in the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and even above and below, bestowing them upon those obstructing *bhūtas*, *nāgas*, *bhairavas*, and the like. Having first recited the mantra to protect oneself and one's companions, ensuring that those obstacles cannot approach, one may then perform the recitation to seek accomplishment.

During the time of recitation, if a corpse stands up and manifests various evil signs, one should know that these are various types of obstacles created by Māras. Once the practitioner has discerned this clearly, they should take white mustard seeds mixed with ashes, recite the *Buddhoṣṇīṣarāja* mantra over them, and throw them at the face of the corpse.
By the great power of the mantra, all those who create obstacles flee in the four directions; once the obstructing māras have departed, the corpse lies as it was before.

If the corpse stands upright without any evil signs, one should know that this is the efficacy of the mantra’s power, and that the sought-after accomplishment will certainly be attained without doubt.

If you attain such [a state], you must first resolve your own mind; then, whatever aspirations the practitioner previously sought, one should declare them all at this time—whether seeking the revelation of hidden treasures (*nidhi*), seeking entry into the Asura caves to fetch sacred medicines, desiring to mount a sword, seeking eye-salve, subduing spirits and deities, or even seeking the favor and esteem of a king—all such matters can be accomplished.
The practitioner must at all times practice the supreme conduct and employ the power of the Great Mantra for self-protection; only then will they achieve success in the Vetāla rite.
Why is this so? It is like a fierce beast that, though powerful, lacks wisdom and is consequently harmed by wicked men.
If a practitioner does not cultivate superior conduct and does not protect themselves, it is likewise the case that they will be taken advantage of by various evil māras and obstacles.

Chapter Eight: The Section on Invoking the *Pātra-deva* to Relate Matters. Furthermore, if one wishes to invoke the *Pātra-deva* to descend and relate matters, there are several locations where that *Pātra-deva* may descend: namely, the fingertips, a copper mirror, clear water, a mass of fire, level ground, lapis lazuli ground, the flame of a lamp, a youth, the midst of space, and various offering vessels; these are all places where the *Pātra-deva* descends.

If there is a practitioner who has invited [the deity] to come, then within the previously described lower abode, the deity will speak of its own experiences in the heavens and the human realm, as well as the past, future, and present, even providing a detailed account of matters such as the good and evil that transcend the three periods of time.

If, at the time of the practitioner’s invocation, they do not follow the ritual procedures and thus fail in the Dharma; or if the mantras they recite contain errors, omissions, or redundancies; or if they lack correct faith and do not study the Mahāyāna sūtras and teachings;
or if they do not present offerings, or if they do offer them, they do not seek out a pure location according to the site;
or if the youth lacks dignified features in his head, face, eyes, hands, feet, or any other part of his body—[in these cases, the rite will not succeed].

If it is thus, although those practitioners may exert themselves with diligence, the bowl will not descend from the heavens; not only will the summoned deity fail to arrive, they will even encounter inauspicious events.
"If a practitioner who maintains the recitation wishes to perform the rite of summoning the *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar), they must first cultivate the preliminary practices (*pūrvasevā*).

As for these preliminary practices: one should first recite the mantra of the *bhadraghaṭa* one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) times, or three hundred thousand times. Thereafter, on an auspicious day during the waxing moon, one should abstain from food and prepare a mixture of purified earth, *gomaya* (cow dung), and other substances to smear upon the ground and construct a mandala the size of a cowhide; this is the place for the lower *bhadraghaṭa*."

If one wishes to perform the rite for a youth, one should first bathe the youth until he is pure and have him don new white garments. Once he has been granted the eight precepts and is purified both internally and externally, he shall sit at the center of the mandala facing west. One should offer incense, flowers, and other articles as worship. The practitioner likewise spreads *kuśa* grass within the mandala and sits facing east, reciting the fundamental mantra of the deity while praying with single-minded devotion; thus, accomplishment will certainly be attained.

If one wishes to cause [the deity] to descend into a mirror, first procure a fine mirror that is perfectly round and free from damage or defects. Rub it with pure ash seven, eight, or ten times until it is polished and bright, then place it at the center of the altar. When the *pātra-devatā* descends, worldly and supramundane matters will immediately manifest within the mirror.
If one wishes to cause the bowl-deity to descend upon the finger, one should first wash and dye the thumb with lac-water, and subsequently rub it with fragrant oil; then the bowl-deity will descend.
If one wishes to cause [the deity] to descend into water, one should take fresh water, filter it, and add it to the vessel; then the bowl-deity will descend into it and manifest the matter at hand.

If one wishes to cause [the deity] to descend upon an empty space, before various sacred images, or into a mass of flames from a lamp, one should first recite the mantra and sprinkle consecrated water; then the vessel-bearing deity (Bhāṇḍadevatā) will immediately descend.

"If one has requested [the bowl] from the aforementioned locations and brought it down, one should immediately present various incenses and flowers as an offering to delight the Bowl Deity (*pātra-devatā*).
Once the deity is delighted, they will then reveal matters of good and evil and so forth within a dream."

If, despite practicing all the dharmas with diligence, the deity does not descend, one should further generate a mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion for the benefit and happiness of others. For one day, one should abstain from food and again receive the eight precepts. Before a sublime and honored image or before a stupa containing relics, one should spread auspicious grass (kuśa), sit upright and straight, and remain motionless and unwavering, focusing the mind single-pointedly. One should recite the mantra of the Mother of the Family or the Lord of the Family one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) times or two hundred thousand times. Once the count is complete, one should perform this rite once more.
When reciting the mantra of the Wrathful King and invoking the syllable *Oṃ*, one can cause even a withered tree to enter [the state of possession], let alone a human being.
"If you wish to cause it to descend upon a child, you should first seek out ten boys or ten girls;
if that number is insufficient, eight, six, four, or two may also suffice."
He must be ten or twelve years of age; furthermore, his physical form must be perfectly complete, with no veins or joints visible anywhere on his body;

his complexion must be bright white, his crown of the head well-proportioned, his hair black, lustrous, and smooth, his face like the full moon, his eyes long and wide, and his teeth even and closely set.
His arms were slender and long, smooth, round, and lovely; his two breasts were full and prominent; the hair on his body curled to the right;
between his heart and navel there were three folds of skin; his navel was deep and level; his waist was slender and straight;
and even his thighs, forearms, knees, calves, ankles, toes, and heels—all these features were perfectly formed and endowed with every mark of excellence. Thus he was a man...
Whatever is seen should be cherished and not abandoned.

If one obtains such a boy or girl, then on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the waxing moon—or another auspicious day—one should first have them bathe for purification, dress them in new white garments or adorn them with garments of pearls.

Once the decorations are complete, he shall confer the eight precepts upon him. Then, he will sit within the mandala facing east; on that day, the practitioner himself shall also abstain from food, bathe until pure, and don new white garments. He shall prepare various kinds of incense, flowers, flower garlands, unguents, burning incense, and lit lamps, as well as various exquisite foods and drinks, to make offerings to the Principal Deity and the celestial deities who protect the eight directions. Furthermore, he shall separately set aside offerings to present to the devas, asuras, and the classes of hidden spirits.
Having performed this, the practitioner further scatters exquisite flowers over that youth, and then, holding an incense burner in hand, recites the mantra of the *pātra-devatā*.

The mantra should begin with the syllable "HŪṂ," followed in the middle by the phrase "KṚṢṆA. At this point, one should cast a flower into the hands of the youth, then recite "ABHIṢIÑCA" three times, and finally recite "KṚṢṆAPRA."
When one recites thus, the *pātra-devatā* will immediately enter the body of the youth in an instant.
One must also carefully observe its signs.

If the youth’s countenance becomes radiant and joyful, his eyes do not blink, and he is without inhalation or exhalation, then one knows that the *pātra-devatā* has already arrived. Thereupon, one may burn incense and offer *argha*; within the mind, one should recollect the mantra of the Supreme Vidyārāja, perform prostrations and offerings, and then inquire:
"Venerable one, what deity are you that you have condescended to come here?
I currently have certain doubts regarding myself and others; I pray that you will explain them to me swiftly.
One must ask immediately and must not hesitate.

Each of those bowl-bearing deities spoke, mostly recounting matters of good and evil throughout the three periods of time; whether it be suffering or happiness, gain or loss, they recounted every variety of such events one by one.
Having spoken thus, you should accept this with faith and harbor no doubts.

Once the matters you have asked have been concluded, you must promptly perform offerings according to the Dharma, express your gratitude, bid him farewell, and request that he return to his original station.

"Furthermore, when the god Pāṃśupradāna himself descends, there shall be signs of verification by which he may be known: he will appear in the form of a youth, his two eyes round and clear, with a slight reddish hue around the black pupils; his face and head will be well-proportioned and his countenance joyful; he will gaze at things without blinking and will be without inhalation or exhalation, possessing the marks of a noble person of great spirit.
If it is thus, then this is truly the god Pāṃśupradāna who has descended."

If an obstructing māra descends, its form is likewise that of a youth; it has no inhalation or exhalation, its countenance is hideous, its eyes are round and mostly red, it assumes an expression of wrathful anger, and it opens its mouth in a terrifying manner.
If one perceives such signs, one should know that these are māras, rākṣasas, nāgas, or classes of hidden-moving spirits; having ascertained this, one must immediately perform rites to expel them.

The practitioner of recitation shall, at the site of the mandala, recite auspicious gāthās, the Sūtra of the Great Powerful Vidyārāja, the Samaya-sūtra, the mantra of the Wrathful Vidyārāja Ucchuṣma, and even various Mahāyāna dhāraṇīs, and thereby dismiss [the deities].

If they do not depart in this manner, one should recite the Mantra of the Lion Throne. Using fuel sticks of *arika* wood and *pāṭala* wood, perform a homa sacrifice one hundred times with clarified butter, honey, curd, and rice blossoms, or sesame seeds and so forth. Thereafter, recite the Mantra of Krodha-Ḍākinī three or seven times while performing the homa; then those obstructing māras will no longer dare to remain and will naturally retreat.

All those who possess wisdom should understand and practice each of these teachings accordingly; if you act for this purpose, do not let your diligent efforts be in vain and devoid of spiritual response.

Chapter Nine: The Section on Explaining the Obstacles and Prohibitions. Furthermore, in the *Sūtra of the Questions of Bodhisattva Subāhu*, the section on explaining the obstacles and prohibitions, chapter nine, the Bodhisattva Subāhu again asked Vajrapāṇi:
"When a practitioner cultivates and recites mantras, what karmic obstructions prevent them from attaining siddhi?"
"I pray that you will proclaim it for us, so that all future practitioners may each come to understand it clearly and be free from doubt regarding these practices.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed Subāhu Bodhisattva, saying: "Subāhu!..."

If there are practitioners who, from past lives until the present life, have been unable to properly guard their body, speech, and mind, thereby committing various grave offenses, for this reason it is difficult for them to achieve success in their Dharma practice.

What are called the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) taught by the Buddha are: killing an Arhat, killing one’s father or mother, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, shedding the blood of a Buddha with a mind of malice, and—furthermore—destroying a Buddha-stūpa; or killing a Bodhisattva; or forcibly defiling the mother of an Arhat through unchaste conduct; or, whether acting on another’s behalf or doing it oneself, coercively seizing the property of the Triple Gem. Such transgressions as these, the Buddha has declared to be the five deeds of immediate retribution.
If such faults exist, it will be difficult to accomplish the Dharma.
Why is this? Because of these grave offenses, one shall fall into hell and undergo suffering for one kalpa before one’s prior transgressions are exhausted; only then can one attain liberation.
Therefore, it is said that although such a person may exert great effort and undergo hardship, due to the obstruction of their karma, they will never achieve success with any mantras.

Furthermore, regarding the sūtras and dharmas spoken by the Tathāgatas, they may—with a mind of hatred—burn them with fire, drown them in water, or otherwise destroy them through various means; or they may slander the Dharma-body, kill monks or nuns who uphold the precepts, or for no reason kill men or women who maintain the precepts; or, out of a hateful mind, they may set fire to and burn monasteries.
If one possesses such offenses, even though they may exert diligent effort, they will not achieve success.

If, at any time, one gives rise to a harmful mind toward the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha—regardless of its magnitude—I shall now describe but a small portion of the retribution such a person receives: that individual shall fall into the Avīci Hell. Once this karmic retribution is exhausted, they will again be born among humans; yet due to residual karma, even if they obtain a human body, they will be born into a poor and lowly lineage. Should they encounter a virtuous friend who exhorts them to resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta, they will later remain unstable, eventually returning once more to take refuge in non-Buddhist deities and the like.
Even though those non-Buddhist deities see him taking refuge, they do not rejoice; instead, they give rise to anger and malice.
For such a person, the practice of recitation and cultivation will ultimately never achieve success.
"Furthermore, if there is anyone who first gives rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, from that time forward, all devas and humans should offer them worship."

Why is this? Because such a person is one who bears the burden of all sentient beings, being able to bestow fearlessness upon them, and even capable of continuing the lineage of the Three Jewels; therefore, they should not return salutations to the various devas.
Furthermore, one must not commit the transgression of causing violent harm or killing a rishi;
nor should one mutually destroy mantras or vidyās;
nor, out of a mind of anger, fail to make offerings to the lords of mantras and vidyās.
Furthermore, some even tread upon lotus flowers and various mudrās with their feet;
or they recklessly break off grasses, trees, and the like with their hands;

or they prostrate before malevolent yakṣas and similar beings; or they consume the remnants of offerings to deities or the remnants of offerings to ghosts and spirits; or they eat food discarded on the ground.
Furthermore, some engage in unchaste acts with female animals, or commit such acts with women in monasteries or other pure places;
or they harm various snakes and insects through the use of incantations or medicinal drugs;
or, riding elephants, horses, oxen, or donkeys, they lash them violently with whips in order to make them move swiftly.
Furthermore, those who do not give rise to a heart of compassion to rescue and aid the sick and those in distress—
such persons shall never achieve accomplishment in mantras and vidyās.
"Furthermore, practitioner, just as space cannot be measured, so too is the retribution experienced by anyone who causes harm toward the Triple Gem; that retribution is likewise immeasurable."
Furthermore, the practitioner may have previously harmed sentient beings with nets, kept cats to catch and kill insects and mice, or even imprisoned birds such as parrots in cages.

Such a person shall not achieve accomplishment, nor shall they be permitted to enjoy offerings dedicated to the Buddha; furthermore, they shall not prostrate before Maheśvara, Sūrya, Candra, Agni, or Nārāyaṇa, even if they encounter hardship or distress, they must not prostrate before them.

One should not recite the teachings of those gods, nor should one make offerings to those who practice such dharmas; one should feel neither aversion nor delight toward those teachings, nor should one approve of their ritual procedures.

If there are those who possess wealth and treasures and wish to practice giving, they should first give rise to the mind of great compassion; they should first pay homage to all Buddhas, and next pay homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
Why is this? Those bodhisattvas are like the new moon; having already surpassed all the luminaries, they will gradually become full and illuminate the world with their brilliance.
Those bodhisattvas are also like this: although they are currently on the stages (bhūmi), they will ultimately realize unsurpassed bodhi. For this reason, one ought to pay homage to such an assembly.

Furthermore, since Bodhisattvas and others are those who bear the burden of all sentient beings, those who give rise to great compassion with the desire to rescue and deliver them should first pay homage to these Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there are in this world certain pitiable beings—foolish and inferior—who are unwilling to prostrate before Bodhisattvas and the like. These Bodhisattvas possess great diligence and their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are difficult to fathom; if a practitioner does not prostrate, not only will they fail to achieve accomplishment in the dharmas they recite, but they will also be showing contempt for all Buddhas.

Why is this? It is like how all fruits in the world are obtained from flowers; the flower is a metaphor for the bodhisattva, and the fruit is a metaphor for bodhi. Therefore, practitioners should faithfully pay homage to them.

If there is a bodhisattva who, for the sake of benefiting others, manifests the practice of desire toward those who are lustful, and so forth, even toward virtuous or evil persons they harbor no actual feelings of love or hatred; rather, out of compassion, they employ skillful means to praise or disparage them.
Why would a practitioner fail to give rise to faith and pay homage to the Bodhisattvas?

Those Bodhisattvas may manifest various forms as mantra-vidyā lords in order to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings; therefore, one must certainly believe in and pay homage to all the masters of mantra-vidyā lords.

10. The Section on Explaining the Supreme Path, from the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Subāhu*, Part Ten: "Furthermore, the practitioner who recites [the mantra] should not give rise to doubt regarding the practice they are performing. They should always take the Eightfold Noble Path as their support; for one who walks this path will certainly attain *siddhi* in the practice of *mantra*.
Moreover, in the future, they shall constantly be born in superior and wondrous places among gods and humans."
The Buddhas of the past cultivated this path and attained perfect enlightenment; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the present and future do likewise.
To cultivate merit through body, speech, and mind, always relying upon the words of the Buddha without giving rise to weariness—such cultivation is called right action.
To have no attachment toward the food, drink, medicine, clothing, bedding, and all other things one uses, is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).

To neither praise nor disparage oneself or others, to remain far removed from anger as if avoiding a mass of fire, and to fear transgressions like a fierce tiger startled by fire—constantly maintaining such a state—is called right conduct (*samyak-karmānta*).

One does not study the divination of men and women or matters of good and bad fortune; one does not study the methods of astronomy, geography, and yin-yang, nor even the arts of subduing dragons, training elephants and horses, calligraphy, arithmetic, archery, and the bow. To be able to distance oneself from such transgressions is called right discernment.

One should not go to watch spectacles such as battles between elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, chickens, cranes, and other birds, nor the games of men wrestling; to be able to remain free from such transgressions is called right mindfulness.

Furthermore, one should not speak of the state, the royal court, or local administration; nor discuss matters of military conflict or warfare; nor engage in talk concerning brothels, courtesans, or sensual attachments; nor speak of riddles; nor speak of events from the past; nor indeed any worldly discourse on useless texts or matters. The practitioner of recitation must distance themselves from all such various faults.

"Furthermore, if one maintains the recitation seeking *siddhi*, until the point of its accomplishment, one should not enter cities, towns, villages, stupas, temples, monasteries, or the shrines and palaces where non-Buddhists reside; one must not go to such places."

If one cannot avoid performing the recitation, one should seek out one of the aforementioned locations as a pure and excellent site; or otherwise, seek a secluded dwelling among the mountains, or by a pond, or an empty house, an old shrine, beneath a tree, on a riverbank, or even beside a mountain spring—a place free from all clamor and devoid of people—where one may focus the mind single-mindedly upon the recitation.

Furthermore, throughout the year, except for the three months of the summer retreat when one does not travel, during the spring rains as well as at other times, one may wander at will through mountain forests, springs, and ponds, or even to any of the aforementioned sublime locations, and there recite with single-minded devotion.
If a practitioner is performing preparatory rites, even if the required number of recitations has been completed, they must not perform the rite of accomplishment during the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

For example, just as a *bhikṣu* performs no activities whatsoever during the summer retreat but remains seated in tranquil stillness, so too is it for the practitioner of recitation; they must not interrupt their recitation at all. Only after the summer retreat is concluded, having protected themselves according to the Dharma, may they then perform the accomplishment.
"Furthermore, those who seek siddhi, having completed the required number of recitations, must perform homa.
There are several types of homa hearths to be constructed, namely: the lotus-shaped, the circular, the triangular, and the square."
These four types have different applications; they must all be manufactured with a devout mind and in accordance with the Dharma.

If one wishes to construct a hearth (*kuṇḍa*), one should first seek pure earth and mix it with *gomaya* (cow dung) to make clay for plastering the hearth. The hearth must have a rim and be made extremely firm; furthermore, one should construct steps on its four sides to serve as the seats for making offerings to the noble sages.
If one performs virtuous deeds, seeks wealth and treasures, or even seeks the pacification of calamities and cherishes the Dharma, one must construct a circular hearth.
If one seeks all manner of objectives, including the service of young maidens and the like, one must construct a lotus-shaped hearth.
If one intends to subdue various nāgas and all classes of spirits, or to cause them to be consumed by fire or to suffer pain, one must construct a square hearth.
If one intends to perform malevolent rites, desiring to cause enemies to feel terror, flee far away, and not dare to approach, one must construct a triangular hearth.

"Once the constructed hearth has been fashioned in accordance with the Dharma and the prescribed ritual, one should spread auspicious grass (śara) all around the four sides of the hearth. All materials for the homa must be placed upon the base outside the hearth where it has been smeared with cow dung (gomaya). Thereafter, one should scatter various flowers, ointments, incense, food offerings, and so forth near that hearth, making offerings to the Three Jewels, as well as to the Great Vajra Family Lords, the Mantra Lords, and others."
Having completed the offerings, one then kindles a fire within the hearth.
The fire must not be blown upon with the mouth; rather, it should be fanned with a fan.

Once the fire has ignited, first take rice blossoms or sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter (*sarpis*), and while reciting the principal mantra of the respective *vidyā*, cast them into the fire—one by one—either seven times, eight times, or up to twenty times. This is called the *homā* offering to the Lord of Mantras.
Having completed the offerings, one should then perform homa according to the ritual rules to seek siddhi.

First, the practitioner must protect themselves by reciting the mantra of Krodha-Ḍākinī over auspicious grass (kuśa) seven, eight, or twenty times, binding it around the neck as a protective amulet. Thereafter, having spread the auspicious grass, one should sit facing east.

Place ghee, honey, curd, and white mustard seeds together in a vessel; using both ends of the wood used for the ritual, recite the mantra of the tutelary deity and cast them into the fire, reciting once for each casting.
"When fire first blazes up, one first observes the flames to discern its auspicious or inauspicious signs."

If this fire ignites spontaneously without being fanned, and becomes intensely blazing without smoke, furthermore, without the sound of crackling and with many peaks of flames arising, turning consistently to the right like the brilliant sun, unobstructed by anything; its color being like gold or coral, its forms diverse—sometimes broad, sometimes long; resembling a rainbow or a flash of lightning, a peacock’s tail or a lotus blossom, a *homa* ladle or a vajra, a trident or a horizontal sword, a banner or a conch shell, a fly-whisk or a chariot; and even the sounds of various musical instruments such as drums and flutes, while its fragrance is like that of burning clarified butter.
If one obtains such various auspicious signs, it should be known that one will swiftly attain vast siddhi.

Furthermore, if the fire at first is difficult to ignite; or if, though ignited, it produces much smoke yet its flames cannot become vast or blazing; or if it gradually subsides, becomes weak, and finally goes out; or even if it does not go out, it mingles with smoke and lacks a red or crimson hue; or if it is like the solar disc within clouds, unable to shine clearly; or if the flames rise upward but take the shape of a bull’s head or resemble the forms of a donkey or a horse; or if they suddenly erupt in a great blaze and scorch the practitioner; or if the fire’s vapor smells like the burning of a corpse—[these are inauspicious].
If the practitioner perceives such signs and realizes they are inauspicious, the *siddhi* sought will certainly not be accomplished.

The practitioner must then once again combine rice blossoms, white mustard seeds, clarified butter, and honey, and perform *homa* while reciting the mantras of the Great Powerful King of the Naked Body (*Vajrapāṇi*) and the Wrathful King of Foul Traces (*Ucchuṣma*), etc.; thus, the previously appearing inauspicious signs will naturally cease to appear and all will be extinguished.

"Furthermore, the practitioner should not shave the hair of the three places with a razor, nor should they apply medicinal ointments to cause it to fall out, nor should they pluck it away with their hands."
For example, if a person holds a sharp blade in their hand, they will quickly injure themselves if they lack wisdom;
likewise, if a person recites mantras without relying on the ritual procedures, not only will the rite fail to achieve its result, but they will also incur further personal harm.

If a practitioner recites and cultivates without following the ritual rules, or fails to maintain the precepts, or remains impure, the Great Lord of Mantras will ultimately not become angry or cause harm; however, because the retinue and attendants of the Lord of Mantras perceive such transgressions, they will immediately inflict injury.

"Furthermore, if a practitioner of recitation desires to attain swift *siddhi*, they must not omit even the slightest detail of the prescribed ritual procedures, lest various māras and obstacles find an opportunity to interfere. One must provide, according to one's means, various foods, drinks, incense, flowers, fruits, and the like, to offer as sacrifices to the devas, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, garuḍas, kinnaras, gandharvas, bhūtas, and all other malevolent spirits, praying for their protection so that no hindrances may arise."

Once the sacrificial offerings have been prepared, one must immediately, with a devout mind, call each deity by name, entreating them to descend individually, accept the offerings, and assist in the accomplishment of *siddhi*.
Then recite this mantra of invocation, which says: "Nīva asura yakṣabhūtagraha-siddhādyakṣa-sūparṇaka-kaṭapūtana-śiṣya."
Dvandva-ghaṇṭā-rākṣasogra-harjita-śīghra-gati-kim-puruṣa-vināśanti-nivartya-svastyayana-bhūti-vardhaye.
Haṃ kṛtavadānavejñāpāyami dantuputradanai sahabūrttya saṃkhe sūrutva iha yantu.
