Chapter Eleven: The Detailed Classification of the Various Sections Furthermore, I shall now, within the Vidyādhara-piṭaka, provide a detailed classification of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth, as well as the mantras, mudrās, and other elements taught in the various sections.
The Tathāgata has taught three koṭis and five lakṣas of mantras, along with the names of their presiding lords; therefore, it is called the Vidyādharapiṭaka.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara has also taught three koṭis and five lakṣas of mantras, and within this section, the name of the mantra lord is Hayagrīva, and he has also taught the various names of the maṇḍalas of his own family.

Furthermore, there are seven mantra-lords; each of these mantra-lords has twelve arms, or six, or four, holding the *Amoghapāśa* (Infallible Lasso) and manifesting transformations at will. Some have four faces and wear jeweled crowns adorned with wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), their radiance shining brilliantly like the sun illuminating the world. These mantra-lords are all governed by the Horse-Headed Maṇḍala.

Furthermore, there are eight vidyārājñīs, namely: Netra-śukla, Māṇibhadra-śukla, Avalokita, Eka-jaṭā, Suvarṇa-mukhī, Yaśasvinī, Bhikṣuṇī, and Koṭi. These are all vidyārājñīs of the Lotus Family (Padmakula). They also proclaim seven koṭis of mantras, along with various maṇḍalas and mudrās, for the benefit of all impoverished sentient beings and for the subjugation of all obstructing spirits and prowling demons.

Furthermore, there are seventeen mantra-kings with sixty-four retinues; additionally, there are eight great heart-mantra kings, as well as various great wrathful vidyārājas, such as Amṛtakuṇḍalī Vidyārāja, Vijayottama Vidyārāja, and Mahāpuṇya Vidyārāja.
This section of mine is called the Vast Vajra Family, in which eight lakṣas of mantras are taught.

Furthermore, there is a great deity named Bhañjika who teaches twenty thousand mantras; that deity has a consort named Mīgarā who teaches ten thousand mantras, which is also called the Bhañjika Family.
Furthermore, there is a great deity named Maṇibhadra who speaks one hundred thousand (lakṣa) mantras.
Additionally, there is the Lord of Wealth who speaks three hundred thousand mantras, known as the Maṇi Family.

Furthermore, there were all those among the devas, humans, asuras, and others who had faith in the Buddha, who immediately uttered immeasurable mantras before the Buddha. These were distributed among the various families (*kula*): some entered my Great Vajra Family, some entered the Great Lotus Family, some entered the Akṣobhya Family, some entered the Bhañjaka Family, and some entered the Maṇi Family; likewise, some entered those not subsumed under any family.
Regarding the various teachings of mantras as explained above, practitioners within these five families may all practice them.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has said:

"There is an inner, supreme, most excellent, and wondrous jewel; moreover, from this flows forth the ultimate jewel of the Dharma, from which the eight great beings (mahāpuruṣa) are born, who are jewels that never regress."
"Such are the Three Jewels; they are the most honored and supreme within the three realms, serving as the great field of merit.

Therefore, practitioners who wish to extinguish transgressions, generate merit, and cause the presence of the deity to swiftly achieve *siddhi*, should first take refuge in these Three Jewels at the time of recitation.

If there are those who uphold and recite the mantras within my Vajra Family, they should first take refuge in the Triple Gem; next, they should first invoke: *Namo Ścaṇḍavajrapāṇaye Mahāyakṣasenāpataye*, and only thereafter recite the mantra.
The same applies to the Padma family; it is likewise for the Ardhaka and Maṇi families.

Furthermore, when a practitioner of recitation performs the recitation, they must first take refuge in the Triple Gem, and next take refuge in the Lord of the Mantra of their own family, before they may recite the root mantra of their chosen practice.

If a practitioner does not place faith in the Buddha, but instead believes only in the teachings of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, their faith is insufficient; furthermore, if they constantly harbor stinginess and envy within their hearts, they shall not be permitted to hold the great vajra taught in my doctrine.

"Furthermore, there may be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who, with wrong views, slander this sublime teaching of the Great Vehicle Mantra, saying it is not the authentic teaching but was spoken by Māra; I declare that such persons are utterly deluded."

Furthermore, they claim that I, the Great Vajrapāṇi, am merely of the yakṣa class and not the true fundamental source; thus, they are unwilling to believe in or pay homage to me, and even refuse to believe in or pay homage to the great bodhisattvas.
Should anyone recite my sublime mantras, they will surely bring about their own ruin before long.

Why is this? Indeed, how could Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others ever harbor malicious intent to harm or afflict sentient beings? It is only because when all the kinsmen and various spirits within their retinues see these deluded people grasping my great Vajra-family *vajra* while simultaneously reciting the sublime mantras of my teachings, those kinsmen will immediately glare at them with wrathful eyes, even to the point of destroying their bodies and lives.

If there are members of the fourfold assembly who are practitioners cultivating the path, constantly reading and reciting the teachings of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna, and furthermore able to analyze and explain them for the sake of all sentient beings; if they possess great diligence, turn the non-retrogressive wheel, and single-mindedly aspire toward unsurpassed bodhi—then you should know that such persons uphold and recite my teachings, and will certainly and swiftly attain the fulfillment of their aspirations.

"Furthermore, I have already previously explained the various teachings on mantras for Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others; you should receive them with single-minded faith and not give rise to any doubts."
I shall now further explain for you the mantra teachings of those worldly and transworldly non-Buddhists, as well as the devas, māras, and Brahmās; you should listen attentively!
Maheśvara spoke ten koṭis of mantras; Nārāyaṇa spoke thirty thousand mantras;
Mahābrahmā spoke sixty thousand mantras; Sūryadeva spoke two lakṣas of mantras;
the host of Śakradevendra spoke eighteen thousand mantras; and Caṇḍika spoke eight thousand mantras.
It is said that Agni spoke three thousand seven hundred mantras; Kubera spoke three thousand mantras;
the various Dragon Kings spoke five thousand mantras; the Lord of Ghosts spoke twelve thousand mantras;
the four World-Protecting Great Kings together spoke four lakṣas of mantras; and the Asura King spoke two lakṣas.
The Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven spoke two hundred thousand mantras; likewise,
each of these deities individually expounded various mantras and mudrās, as well as maṇḍala rituals and so forth, which may be received and maintained according to the Dharma.
If one violates the original teachings, not only will the mantras fail to achieve accomplishment, but one will also incur faults and transgressions for oneself. **Chapter Twelve:

The Exposition of the Eight Methods from the *Sūtra Asked by Subāhu Bodhisattva*** "Furthermore, the methods for accomplishment are comprised of eight kinds in total. They are: the method for accomplishing mantras, the method for attaining longevity, the method for the accomplishment of medicines, the method for extracting hidden treasures (*nidhi*), the method for entering the palaces of the asuras, the method for synthesizing gold, the method for transforming earth into gold, and the method for producing priceless jewels."
These eight methods are categorized into three grades:
achieving mantras, attaining longevity, and entering the palaces of the asuras—these three constitute the superior grade;
achieving priceless jewels, revealing hidden treasures, and transforming earth into gold—these three constitute the middling grade.
The synthesis of gold and the accomplishment of medicinal elixirs—these two constitute the inferior grade.

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings whose wisdom surpasses that of ordinary men and who possess the virtue of precepts, and who also delight in practicing the Mahāyāna Dharma, such persons may seek the superior grade.
Moreover, if there are sentient beings who, though possessing the practice of cultivation, have not yet ceased their craving and desire, they may seek the middling grade.
Furthermore, if sentient beings are deluded, they will inevitably seek inferior grades.
Those practitioners who, despite undergoing all manner of poverty and suffering, are constantly lacking, should seek middling grades rather than inferior ones.
If one wishes to obtain the various accomplishments of the eight dharmas, one must cultivate merit as a supporting foundation.

For those who possess merit, whatever they seek—whether the happiness of gods and humans, all manner of delights, longevity, preeminent power and dignity, or physical beauty and intelligence—all such qualities will be fully accomplished.

If there is a practitioner who does not cling to worldly pleasures but delights in cultivation, who constantly keeps the Triple Gem in mind, who perpetually and fully observes the rules of mantra practice, and who never interrupts their recitation—such a person will surely achieve accomplishment, extinguish karmic obstacles, and be liberated from all sufferings.
"Furthermore, that which can bring about all forms of happiness in both the present and the future is none other than the power of the mantras spoken by the Buddha; there is no other method."

Just as when a celestial fire descends or frost and hail fall, they can damage plants and trees with no way to escape them; so too is it with the power of mantras, which can destroy suffering and all obstacles of sin.

Furthermore, just as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) can fulfill all the aspirations of sentient beings, so too is the power of mantra able to bestow upon sentient beings all *siddhis*, as well as wealth, beauty, strength, and long life.

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas observe sentient beings encountering calamities from kings, or disasters of water and fire, or even the perils of being plundered and killed by bandits—when they are oppressed by all manner of fears and sufferings—the Bodhisattvas immediately transform themselves into the various forms and appearances of the Mantra Kings to rescue these sentient beings and bring them to liberation.

"Furthermore, although sentient beings dwelling in the household life may be attached to exquisite sensory objects, if they daily recite the mantras and their ritual procedures—even if not with fierce diligence—and thus complete the required number of preliminary practices (*pūrvasevā*) over a long period;

once these preliminaries are fulfilled and signs manifest before them, they should at that time renounce the five desires and, being pure in their observance of the precepts, enter a quiet chamber to recite the mantra for one *lakṣa*. Thereafter, before long, they will attain the *siddhi* they desire."
"Furthermore, when a practitioner is engaged in recitation or at the time of attaining *siddhi*, they enter the maṇḍala to approach the various worthy sages.
Having cultivated this dharma, it is essential that they remain pure."

Regarding the method of bathing: first, one should mix pure earth with clean water and smear it all over the body; thereafter, one enters the great waters to bathe as desired. Having cleansed the hands and feet, one should sit in a squatting posture facing either east or west and perform the rite for protecting the body.

Immediately take water with the right hand and sprinkle it over the entire body, ensuring that the water makes no sound. Again, take a palmful of water with the right hand, making sure there are no bubbles within the water in the palm. Then, recite the mantra three times over the water in the palm, inhaling three times, likewise without making any sound.
Thereafter, take water and wipe the mouth twice with the thumb, and sprinkle it over the body as a protection.
If, subsequently, one suddenly perceives something coarse or impure within the teeth, or touches them with the hand, or immediately coughs, spits, or sneezes;

or if one feels the breath becoming obstructed or belching occurs, one must again perform the aforementioned rite of reciting mantras over water, drinking the water, wiping the mouth, and rinsing the mouth.
Having finished bathing, one shall immediately enter the quiet chamber; thereafter, one must not engage in conversation with anyone at random, except for one's companions.

Whether they be men or women, whether householders or those who have left the home life, whether followers of external paths, Brahmins of pure conduct, boys, girls, or even the elderly, and even including those of indeterminate gender—none of such persons as these shall be permitted to converse with one another or to come into physical contact.
If one comes into physical contact with another, one must again perform the aforementioned bathing, as well as wiping and rinsing the mouth.

If there is a practitioner who constantly delights in purity, bathes their body, enjoys reciting mantras, possesses universal compassion for all sentient beings, does not give rise to craving or attachment toward the gains and offerings of others, and dwells in solitude begging for food while cultivating the practice of true words—such a person will naturally obtain this sublime dhāraṇī.

"Furthermore, if a practitioner seeks siddhi, should anyone come during the time of recitation to offer excellent garments, gold, silver, precious jewels, ornaments, mounts, unguents, incense, or even food and drink and all manner of articles of pleasure—whether in small or large quantities—he must not accept them at all."

"Furthermore, when a practitioner seeks accomplishment, whenever they have finished either a small or a large evacuation, they must in each instance wash themselves repeatedly with water and earth according to the Dharma to achieve purification."
If one does not eat, this is the most excellent course, as it avoids causing defilement to taint the worthy and holy ones.

"Furthermore, when a practitioner seeks accomplishment, they should fear that their karmic obstacles will prevent them from attaining presence; therefore, they must beforehand perform recitations repeatedly and extend their repentance."

For example, during the heat of summer, when the wind shakes many trees, fire is produced by the friction of the wood against one another; without further effort being applied, it spontaneously consumes the surrounding grasses.
In the same way, when practitioners use the wind of diligence to shake the tree of pure precepts, the fire of recitation arises and likewise burns away the weeds of transgressions.
Furthermore, just as snow that has accumulated and frozen during winter naturally melts away when struck by the sun's rays;
so too, when a practitioner is pure and the sun of the precepts radiates its light, the snow of their transgressions is entirely eliminated.
Furthermore, it is like a thousand-year-old darkness within a room that vanishes entirely when a single lamp suddenly illuminates it;

likewise, the dark karma accumulated over a thousand lifetimes by a practitioner is completely incinerated by the brilliance and majestic power of the lamp of recitation ignited by the fire of wisdom.

"Furthermore, if a practitioner who maintains the recitation and performs the practice—even up to the homa—does not attain siddhi, they should take fragrant mud mixed with pure sand and, at a superior location such as the bank of a river or the side of a spring or pond, fashion one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) stupas using seals, visualizing them as being identical to stupas containing the relics of the Tathāgata."

By virtue of this devout mind, all karmic obstacles created by the practitioner since beginningless time will be completely extinguished, and the siddhi of the sought-after mantra will certainly be attained in the present life.

"Furthermore, for a practitioner of mantra recitation seeking *siddhi*, taking up the precepts is the foundation. Thereafter, they should cultivate the bodhicitta and exert the power of diligence and heroic effort; they must recite the mantras without ever flagging or retreating, and generate redoubled reverence and faith toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
For example, just as a Wheel-Turning King must possess the seven treasures before he can govern his realm in peace and security;

so too, a practitioner who recites mantras must maintain pure observance of the precepts and cultivate even greater reverence and faith toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. If one possesses these qualities, their karmic obstacles will be extinguished and they shall attain *siddhi*.

Furthermore, when a practitioner cultivates the preliminary rites, they should take frequency as paramount; once the number of recitations is complete, they should perform homa. Because of this homa, the deity will become pleased, and thus the practitioner will attain the desired accomplishment regarding their objective.
Furthermore, if a practitioner performs the rite for summoning joyful beings, whatever they desire—even from as far as a hundred yojanas away—all those who come will be yakṣī women.
Furthermore, if there is someone who wishes to accomplish the rite of a yakṣiṇī, even if they attain siddhi, it is not particularly sublime.

For example, just as people in the world display their female beauty to others for the sake of desire, seeking primarily wealth and treasures rather than anything else, so too is it with that yakṣiṇī. She transforms her physical form and seeks out the practitioner; she serves and provides for him in every way without fail, yet this is fundamentally not out of affection, but solely because she is constrained by the power of the mantra.

When that yakṣī comes to serve the practitioner, although she dwells with him and her service is without transgression, her evil intent remains ever-present as she constantly watches for his shortcomings; once she finds a lapse, she immediately causes him harm.

There are those who, out of delusion and for the sake of desire, seek this siddhi; they not only commit the transgression of practicing perverse conduct themselves, but also contravene the four great vows of all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all other noble sages.
Who among the wise would so openly commit such a transgression?

All the devas, humans, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas, and even the bhūtas and various classes of spirits, out of their deep faith and reverence for the Buddha and for the sake of his benefit, spoke their own vidyās before the World-Honored One, entreating the Buddha to grant them his certification and approval; the Buddha, through his compassionate vows, accepted them all.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, for the sake of all sentient beings in the future who are without a protector and without reliance, you have analytically explained the cultivation of the practices of true conduct and speech, so that they may attain the three grades of results: superior, middling, and inferior.

As for the superior grade of fruit, one attains supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), entering the caves of the asuras to conceal one's body at will; one may transform into the husband of a yakṣī, or become a sacred medicine, or immediately transform into Guhyapada and others, or act as the lord of a realm of spirits, or manifest in wrathful form to subdue all ghosts, spirits, and planetary deities (*graha*).
Those of middling capacity seek long life, or seek love and respect, or seek noble status, or seek wealth.

Those of inferior capacity, by means of the power of the Dharma and the efficacy of mantras and medicines, treat all classes of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and bhūtas, as well as the hidden-moving spirits who cause possession and illness; or they use the power of mantras to treat all poisons, or through prohibitions and bindings eliminate all types of poison, or remove diseases caused by medicinal toxins.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"In all the worlds, there are venomous snakes, non-venomous snakes, and various insects of immeasurable kinds.
To speak briefly, they are comprised of four general categories: namely, those with one fang, two fangs, three fangs, and four fangs."

These four categories are divided into eighty types: twenty types move with their heads held high; six types remain stationary and coil their bodies; twelve types, though they sting, are non-venomous; thirteen types are kings of snakes; and the remaining ones are semi-snake, semi-insect species.
"Furthermore, there are various kinds of venomous insects, namely frogs, spiders, and *yūthas*, and the number of such creatures is still great."
However, these insects possess six kinds of venom:
first, the venom of feces, which causes the poison to erupt as soon as it touches a person;
second, the venom of urine, which causes the poison to erupt as soon as it touches a person's body.
Third is the poison of touch, which causes venom to erupt as soon as it touches a person's body;
fourth is the poison of saliva, which causes venom to erupt as soon as a person is touched by saliva;
fifth is the poison of the eye, which causes venom to erupt as soon as the eyes look upon a person.
Sixth is the venom of the fangs, which causes the poison to manifest immediately at the site of the bite.
Regarding the four types of snakes previously mentioned, their venoms vary in depth and intensity:
when bitten by one type, there is a single fang mark; this contains only a trace of venom and is termed a "scratch."
That which is bitten by two fangs has two tooth marks; where blood flows out, it is called "blood-stained.
That which is bitten by three fangs has three tooth marks; when the injury is most severe, it is called "wounded."

Although those of these three types may be saved despite their venom, those bitten by the four-fanged [snake] bear four tooth marks; the poisonous affliction pervades their entire body, and they are certain to proceed toward death, which is termed "the end of life.
As for this fourth type, there may be those who recover through the power of the Dharma.
However, when one is struck by various poisons, the power of mantras surpasses that of medicinal remedies.
Why is this? It is like a great fire that has broken out; if it encounters a heavy rain, the fire is extinguished. The power of the Great Mantra in subduing all types of poison is likewise so.
All those who possess wisdom and well understand these various poisons constantly recite the mantra of great majesty; they play with the poisons together, free from all fear.
Why is this? It is just as when a lion plays with an ox; it is likewise so.

Furthermore, there are various types of malevolent spirits—such as celestial spirits (*deva*), *asura* spirits, *yakṣa* spirits, *nāga* spirits, *gandharva* spirits, *preta* spirits, and even *piśāca* spirits—who either seek offerings, or seek to mock and toy with people, or desire to kill them. For these reasons, they roam the world, constantly devouring flesh and blood, waiting for human transgressions.

Furthermore, it may be due to anger that they strike or seize sentient beings; or due to the affliction of hunger that they disturb sentient beings; or cause them to have their minds deranged, or to sing, dance, rejoice, or grieve; or to become immediately sorrowful and distressed, or to speak incoherently. By performing such various and strange acts, they cause people to feel wonder and laughter.
One should treat them with mantras such as the Vajrāṅkuśa or the Amṛtakuṇḍalī-vajra, and they will immediately be cured.

Furthermore, having foreknowledge of the nature of those various malevolent spirits and the methods for their treatment, one may proceed fearlessly to subdue them, provided that one applies the mantras spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Why is this? There are no mantras of the devas that possess the power to destroy the power of the mantras of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others.

"Furthermore, I shall now further explain the method for extinguishing transgressions. If there is a practitioner who wishes to cultivate this dharma, they should go to a secluded, pure place near a river and construct a *caitya* using fragrant mud mixed with sand, placing within it the sublime verses of the Dharmakāya."

When Brahmā, all the gods, yakṣas, vidyādhara maharṣis, and even the classes of garuḍas, gandharvas, bhūtas, and others behold him, they pay homage with respectful faith; all join their palms and speak thus:
"How marvelous! How marvelous is this one of great compassion!"
Out of compassion for all sentient beings who are without support or refuge, you perform such deeds.
How rare, how rare, O subtle practitioner!
Out of compassion for sentient beings, you perform such deeds.

By the power of the Dharma, those devas may see the practitioner holding a brilliantly blazing great golden vajra, or see him holding a solid iron mallet, or see him holding a fierce and sharp great wheel, or see him holding the Amoghapāśa lasso, or see him holding a three-pronged great trident, or see him holding a sharp sword, or see him holding a staff or a single-pronged fork; or they may see him equipped with various extraordinary and terrifying weapons, or see his countenance as exceptionally handsome and majestic—whosoever sees him feels joy and delight.
Those gods and even the bhūtas spoke these words: "We take refuge in the Venerable One;
before long, we shall surely attain the status of great vidyādhara sages, and even lesser matters such as wealth and prosperity."

If there are those who practice such a true Dharma, they will swiftly attain the eradication of their karmic obstacles and suffer no great pain; they shall shine upon the world like the appearance of the sun.
"We shall protect such practitioners as these, ensuring their minds do not become distracted, until they attain their desired accomplishments.
Having spoken these words, the Brahmā deities and others were all greatly rejoiced; they prostrated with their heads at his feet and each departed, withdrawing to their respective seats.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed Subāhu Bodhisattva, saying: "Subāhu!
You have already heard what I have now spoken; you may cause it to circulate throughout the world for the sake of saving and delivering beings."

Then, the Bodhisattva Subāhu received and undertook to practice it; having prostrated himself, he withdrew and immediately propagated and expounded it widely throughout the world for the sake of sentient beings.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Subāhu, Scroll Four.
